name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri activists want fewer cameras on citizens and more on politicians
description: Pulaski County Sheriff Stacy Ball thinks Flock cameras help his deputies fight crime. But he also thinks they’re not worth keeping. Ball recently announced his office was pulling the plug on Flock Safety, the network of cameras that photographs license plates and gives police a database they can search later — and which has come […]
text:
Flock Safety cameras are mounted on a pole in the parking lot of the Home Depot in Salt Lake City (Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch).Pulaski County Sheriff Stacy Ball thinks Flock cameras help his deputies fight crime.
But he also thinks they’re not worth keeping.
Ball recently announced his office was pulling the plug on Flock Safety, the network of cameras that photographs license plates and gives police a database they can search later — and which has come increasingly under bipartisan fire across the country.
As far as Ball knows, his deputies never abused the system. He believes they used it responsibly. But he’s been hearing from residents worried about privacy, government surveillance and what could happen if the technology fell into the wrong hands.
In the end, that mattered more.
“Your voice matters. Your rights matter. Your trust matters,” he wrote.
Elsewhere in Missouri, the concerns of Flock critics aren’t hypothetical.
The St. Charles County Police Department shut down its network this month after discovering a civilian employee had used the database for a personal, non-law-enforcement purpose. The employee was put on unpaid leave and resigned after being notified the department intended to fire them. The misuse was uncovered after Flock rolled out a tool that flags unusual search patterns.
In Joplin, an officer left the department in January after an investigation found the system had been improperly used. Activists who reviewed the records said the officer accounted for roughly a quarter of the department’s Flock searches and ran one license plate about 395 times, typically listing “DWI” or “Warrants” as the reason without attaching a case number.
That helps explain why Flock has found plenty of skeptics in Missouri, especially among grassroots conservatives.
And they’ve picked up influential allies along the way.
“Americans do not surrender their privacy rights when they drive to work, drop their kids off at school, or go to church,” U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri said last week.
At the same time many of those conservatives are pushing back against Flock cameras in their communities, they’re demanding a camera be turned on in one particular place: the Missouri Senate.
For years, activists have wanted the Missouri Senate to livestream its proceedings. You can listen to the Senate online, but you can’t watch senators debate on the floor. It remains one of only two legislative chambers in the country where that’s true.
State Sen. Mike Moon, an Ash Grove Republican, has repeatedly tried to change it. This spring, his proposal died in circumstances that would have been a little too on the nose if someone had written them into a screenplay.
Senators voted 12-11 to table Moon’s proposal using a standing division. That’s when senators physically rise from their desks to be counted, so there was no roll call showing who voted which way.
The Senate does record video of its proceedings, though, mostly for internal use. The conservative group Act for Missouri filed a Sunshine Law request, paid $6 and got a copy.
And at the point in the video when senators stood up to vote on whether Missourians should be able to watch the Senate, the screen went black.
Perfect.
Moon, as it happens, is also among a bipartisan group of lawmakers who sponsored legislation this year restricting state and local governments from using automated license plate readers.
The two positions may look contradictory, but the argument isn’t really over whether cameras are good or bad. It’s over on which side of the lens government belongs.
Police argue Flock cameras help them find stolen cars, missing people and suspects. But the cameras don’t wait until police suspect you of something. They photograph the cars that pass by and keep the information so police can search it later.
The Missouri Senate works the other way around.
These are elected officials conducting public business in a public building. Yet the Senate keeps video of that work largely for itself. If citizens want to see it, they have to ask, wait and sometimes pay for it.
Put the two fights next to each other and the politics make more sense. The government should have to justify watching you. You shouldn’t have to justify watching the government.
Maybe Missouri doesn’t have a camera problem.
Maybe the cameras are just pointed the wrong way.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: OPINION: ‘Summery’ check in with voters
description: The Nebraska Legislature doesn’t convene for another four months, but a fresh look at what’s on voters’ minds is always helpful. That was clear at a recent legislative candidate forum in Lincoln. Six hopefuls shared the stage, answering questions primarily about environmental issues and then staying around to answer even more questions one-on-one. You know [[...]
text:
Data centers operate in Oregon in 2024. Some states are scaling back their data center incentives as the facilities contribute to increasing electric bills and raise environmental concerns. (Photo by Rian Dundon/Oregon Capital Chronicle)The Nebraska Legislature doesn’t convene for another four months, but a fresh look at what’s on voters’ minds is always helpful. That was clear at a recent legislative candidate forum in Lincoln.
Six hopefuls shared the stage, answering questions primarily about environmental issues and then staying around to answer even more questions one-on-one. You know … what they do in democracies.
That, plus you have to admire those who put themselves on the ballot these days, given the growing disdain throughout the precincts for government, politics and our institutions in general. So kudos to candidates Caitlin Knutson in District 2, incumbent Sen. George Dungan in District 26, former state Sen. Patty Pansing Brooks in District 28, Janet Bock in District 30, Shay Smith in District 32 and incumbent Sen. Danielle Conrad in District 46.
The evening was also a welcome respite from the miasma of our headlines: nonsense about renaming a Great Lake; further bad news on the inextricable quagmire with Iran; the increased cost of everything and now even more so if it has with a maple leaf stamped on it; measles deaths and explosive diarrhea; tainted meat and vaccine vagaries; and bad actors apparently hijacking the petition process in Nebraska. It’s exhausting.
The forum was a live, eyeball-to-eyeball affair, where each of the sextet acquitted themselves well on a variety of topics from clean energy to water quality to the consequences of climate change. These particular candidates — none of whom had their opponents on the dais with them — shared plenty of common ground. Still, it’s always instructive to hear personal perspectives, especially knowing from where they glean the information they use to develop a position or an opinion.
Whoever arrives at the Legislature the first week in January will be faced with a daunting task: addressing the 2027-2029 budget, which at this writing calls to mind images of the Red Sea as deficits approach the B-word. Thirteen of 49 senators will not be returning, whether via term limits or choice. That means in this election Nebraska voters have a chance to loosen the numerical headlock a supermajority can have on the legislative process.
The next Legislature will obviously be focused on extracting the state from its self-inflicted budget crisis. I’m guessing our annual head scratching over property taxes will fill a few days and weeks, too, but, if history serves — and it usually does — few will be satisfied with the outcome. Voting access, education and a myriad of other subjects will fill the chamber from Jan. 6, 2027, to about the first of June.
According to my reading of the candidates’ responses, two issues senators will be addressing next session emerged front and center at the forum: data centers and undoing the looting of the Environmental Trust Fund.
Apparently data centers, built to fuel the AI boom, are on the minds of many Nebraskans on whose doors the candidates have been knocking. They don’t want them. Government leaders, including in Nebraska, who had championed data centers to supply big tech its sustenance have also heard the ruckus opponents are making and slowed or backtracked incentives to bring the water-guzzling, power-sucking, heat-generating facilities to their neighborhoods.
Of course, the argument for data centers is that without them, we’ll fall behind in the AI race, an ill-defined contest that apparently will determine our future as a country or a species … something along those lines. On the way to securing this victory, we’re told, AI will make our lives more productive and efficient while simultaneously rendering many of our jobs obsolete.
That’s a lot to think about. Nebraska voters should demand their legislators do just that.
Finally, while a Lancaster County District judge has put a temporary kibosh on the process, no one among the candidates had anything remotely good to say about the recent budgetary practice of taking constitutionally protected money from the Environmental Trust Fund to essentially pay the state’s bills, using a sort of governmental procedural pass-through. A bill in the last session of the Legislature that would have put a constitutional amendment reaffirming the shielding of the trust’s funds on the ballot this November failed to advance. Is it just me or does it seem odd to have to amend the state constitution to say what it already says?
Not to belabor the point but to put the raiding of the trust’s money in apostolic proportions, Paul was depositing a check (ironically still not enough to cover his bills) while Peter was filing a police report for theft.
Meanwhile, early voting starts soon, so a glimpse about what’s on the minds of candidates — and voters — gives a fresh take on Nebraska’s axiom of citizen watchfulness.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Is a win a win among Oklahoma’s divided GOP electorate? Mike Mazzei is about to find out.
description: Congratulations and good luck to Mike Mazzei. He’s going to need it, as last week’s election results show. Mazzei won the Oklahoma GOP gubernatorial primary runoff by just over 2,000 votes.  A win may be a win, but in this case it should serve as a warning to both Mazzei’s campaign and the state Republican […]
text:
Mike Mazzei addresses his supporters on Tuesday, August 25, 2026, during his watch party in Tulsa, Okla. Mazzei secured the Republican nomination for Governor of Oklahoma by defeating Gentner Drummond.
(Photo by Ace Cuervo/For Oklahoma Voice)Congratulations and good luck to Mike Mazzei.
He’s going to need it, as last week’s election results show. Mazzei won the Oklahoma GOP gubernatorial primary runoff by just over 2,000 votes. 
A win may be a win, but in this case it should serve as a warning to both Mazzei’s campaign and the state Republican party.
In 20 years of covering elections, I have never seen the outcome of a statewide race so close. The fact that it was reveals how fractured the Republican voting base really is, and that Mazzei will have a tough time getting the deeply divided rest of the state to coalesce behind his vision for our future. 
Heading into the primary election season, Mazzei took the traditionally conservative stance in highlighting that he believes human life begins at conception. He wants to eliminate Oklahoma’s income tax and abolish property taxes for veterans and senior citizens. And he wants expanded access to a tax credit program in which state taxpayers pay for wealthy families’ children to attend private school.
Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond, who lost in the primary runoff, laid out a more moderate path forward, with different priorities. 
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Cyndi Munson put it best in a press release after polls closed on Aug. 25. Drummond, she said, campaigned on the issues we’re all facing — “struggling public schools, lack of access to healthcare, and rising costs of groceries, utility bills and other needs of everyday Oklahomans.” He wanted to invest more, not less in public schools.
It’s clear from last week’s election that Oklahomans are wondering if far-right policies – encapsulated by Mazzei – are serving us well.
The evidence says no.
Our rural hospital infrastructure is collapsing. A recent report found that 45 hospitals are at risk of closing — the third most in the nation.
We continue to have a mass exodus of quality educators. Even though our Legislature micromanages schools with mandatory recess time and high-stakes reading testing, we somehow don’t have the adequate policies — or compensation — that incentivizes teachers to remain. 
Access to mental health treatment is lagging, and we have some of the highest suicide rates in the nation.
We also have an exceptionally high poverty rate, which is straining our social service providers, our Medicaid system, and non-governmental nonprofits, like churches and food banks that have been forced to step in to fill the gap.   
Whoever wins in November’s general election will inherit this disaster that has progressively gotten worse under Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt the past eight years.
As the face of the GOP, Oklahoma’s over 1.2 million registered Republicans will be looking to Mazzei for a plan to fix this — and fast. And it better be a plan to solve the real issues because the tired tropes of attacking marginalized groups of people like trans kids and immigrants and fighting against abortion access are no longer unifying the Republican base.
Speaking of the base, you may be wondering where President Donald Trump fits into the picture for Oklahoma. He endorsed Mazzei ahead of the June primary election.
Mazzei made sure to thank the president for that during his election night victory speech. Unsurprisingly, he did not acknowledge why almost as many Republicans picked Drummond in spite of Trump’s endorsement.
Perhaps Mazzei’s supporters like Trump more than Mazzei’s plans.
Lawmakers would do well to remember that if the time comes to consider implementing Mazzei’s ideas. 
Trump may have the influence to be a kingmaker from the White House, but Oklahomans of all walks of life are living in a reality where Drummond’s platform spoke to them.
As Drummond said to Mazzei in his concession speech: “You have to show up for the farmers and ranchers. The small business owners and the working families. And you have to show up for the Oklahomans who didn’t vote for you.”
That includes, hundreds of thousands of registered independents who were locked out of weighing in on this race solely because they’re unaffiliated with any recognized political party, 
One last thing to consider: As Munson’s statement alluded, Democrats aren’t mad at the prospect of facing Mazzei in reliably red Oklahoma 
Their longshot odds of winning the governor’s office in November just went up a slight tick.
Mazzei’s GOP victory leaves open a crack in the door that Munson could take advantage of. To do that, she’ll need to figure out how to get Oklahoma voters to overlook the dreaded “Democrat” that will appear by her name.
That’s a tall order for anyone. But if Mazzei is unable to appeal to more moderate voters and develop a strategy to navigate our way out of our current morass, some voters may just hold their noses and vote for the Democrat come November. 
Or they might just stay home.
So, again, let me wish Mazzei luck over the next few months. 
He’s going to need it.

name: WyoFile
title: ‘I made a promise to myself’: How higher education is transforming lives in Wyoming prisons
description:
Students at Lusk prison graduate with University of Wyoming bachelor’s degrees, the first group to reach this milestone under a program that offers higher education to incarcerated people. 
The post ‘I made a promise to myself’: How higher education is transforming lives in Wyoming prisons appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
LUSK—One spring afternoon when the sun beamed down on the Wyoming Women’s Center, a prison in Lusk, six students sat in a fluorescent-lit room with laptops open before them. A brown and gold University of Wyoming banner with a cowboy on a bucking bronc hung on the far wall. 
“So, who’s going first?” asked Rob Colter, a gray-bearded UW philosophy professor. “Final presentation. Create your own festival.” 
One of the students, Taylor Nicks, snapped her fingers in approval. 
“First victim,” Colter said, waiting for a volunteer.
It was their last day of class on heavy metal philosophy, and a few months before graduation. The course was one of many the students, who wore their orange prison uniforms to class, took to earn their four-year bachelor’s degrees in general studies from the University of Wyoming. Earlier this month, the six women finally reached that finish line, making them the first cohort in Wyoming to earn bachelor’s degrees through a university program called Pathways from Prison. 
Kelly Turner, who wore a small cross on a chain around her neck, volunteered to go first. She handed out flyers with the name of her festival — Metal for the Ages — handwritten in a red, white and blue steampunk font. A skull in a black top hat, one eye socket framing the American flag, grinned below the title. The flyers featured a long list of metal artists — Beyond the Black, Slipknot, Jinjer, Spiritbox, Unleash the Archers, Face Yourself, Nervosa. 
Student Kelly Turner shows her peer, Taylor Nicks, a festival poster she created during their last day of class on heavy metal philosophy at the Wyoming Women’s Center in Lusk on May 14, 2026. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
“Our country was built on freedom, and as we have learned through this class and other philosophy classes, freedom is mostly a figment of your mind. The only way you can really be free is how you see yourself,” Turner told her peers, gesturing with her hands. “The freedom that they have to express themselves through the arts is beautiful, even if they’re kind of scary looking.” 
The students laughed. 
“So, your theme is freedom, is that right?” Colter asked. “Are there specific ways in which some of these bands talk about freedom?” 
“A lot of them talk about politics,” Turner said. “We just listened to the Lamb of God song that was about being so tied up into technology that we are not free.” 
“Metallica talks about politics quite a little bit in their music,” a student added. 
“Jinjer too,” another said. 

University of Wyoming philosophy professor Rob Colter, the director of Wyoming Pathways from Prison, laughs during a class on heavy metal philosophy at the Wyoming Women’s Center in Lusk on May 14, 2026. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

In 2022, the U.S. Department of Education chose Wyoming Pathways from Prison — UW’s prison education initiative, which Colter heads — to be one among about 200 programs in the country participating in the Second Chance Pell Experiment, an Obama administration initiative that opened Pell Grant eligibility for some prison inmates. 
Before the federal initiative, the Pathways from Prison program offered free  UW courses to people in Wyoming prisons, but the courses didn’t culminate in any degree. Extra funding from the Second Chance Pell Experiment has helped the program offer a four-year UW degree in general studies for people incarcerated here.
Research suggests that participation in any form of educational program in prisons decreases the likelihood of recidivism — by about 7 to 15%, according to one paper — and increases the likelihood of being employed after release. But for the six students at the Wyoming Women’s Center, most of whom have long or life sentences, the program provided more than an avenue for employment in the world outside the prison’s walls. It gave them a way to “be an example” for their children and peers, as well as a sense of purpose that was like “giving a lifeline to someone who is drowning,” as Nicks later described in her graduation speech. 
The next student up, Nicks, discovered something in her research about mosh pits that “outraged” her: “I read an article that quoted a new slogan that misogynistic men have been passing around. It was ‘No Clit in the Pit.’” Nicks, who has long, black hair and music notes tattooed on her arm, decided to parody the slogan, calling her festival “Mo’ Clit in the Pit.” 
“This festival is all about empowering women within the metal community not only to jump into the mosh pits with the boys, but in life also,” Nicks said. “This is going to be a two-day festival that includes some of the baddest female artists.” 
The festival would take place at the Women’s Rights National Historical Park on July 19 and 20 — the same dates as the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention, the first formal women’s rights convention held in the U.S. “We have come a long way since this time,” Nicks continued. “In 2026, women have the right to vote, work, run for office. And we damn sure have the right to mosh.” 
Lorrie Hood, reading her notes from index cards, created a festival called Hood Fest. She was raised thinking that metal and those who listened to it “were evil, demonic.” But the philosophy class showed her that this music expresses the stories of real people and the struggles they endure. Amy Doerr’s festival, Synthetica, represented the synthesis of different cultures from bands across 13 countries. The festival featured a square with vendors and guest speakers, including Colter, who would give a talk on metal as a philosophy of life. 
“Hope you’re available,” she joked with her professor. 
From left to right: Paulette Iliff, Lorrie Hood and Amy Doerr look at a flyer created by their peer, Kelly Turner, on their last day of class on heavy metal philosophy at the Wyoming Women’s Center in Lusk on May 14, 2026. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
Paulette Iliff’s festival would take place on a cruise ship traveling through ports in the Caribbean — a route she had taken herself years before. “We’re going to have meet and mingle with your favorite performers, growling seminars,” — the class cheered — “head banging lessons, picks and sticks with guitar and drum lessons, and that will be done, yes, with Scott Ian and Tommy Lee.” 
Sharay Burnett’s festival, Odd Fellows, would “celebrate all of what society deems as odd.” “It’s an affirmation of myself and of the struggle that some of these band members and bands have gone through, and that we have come out on the other side,” Burnett said. The festival would be “metal tie only,” instead of black tie. The students burst into laughter. “That seems dangerous for mosh pits,” Colter commented. 
Throughout the presentations, the students played clips of music from various artists. A woman mopping the floor outside the classroom hummed along to one song. 
More than four years ago, the students sat in a room across the hall making their case for being a part of this program to a panel of UW faculty. As a cohort, they decided what they wanted their general studies degree to focus on, landing on anthropology and psychology. Their coursework included classes in math, the philosophy of Socrates, psychopathy, Spanish, theater, the psychology of death and dying. They often studied together in the classroom or the room next door. “For math, we’ve been down here every night,” one student said. Several of them hope to one day pursue graduate degrees.
“So, I really appreciate how much thought you all put into those presentations,” Colter said at the end of class. “It was clear that you were thinking about how stuff fits together, and there were some pretty creative options. I think the boat would destroy me.” The students laughed. 
Colter then posed a question: “What do you think this class was about?” 
The students threw out a list of words: Politics, activism, culture, thinking, subversion, imagery, community. Writing, researching, questioning. 
“I don’t think we’ve hit it,” one student laughed. 
“What it is for me is learning on a deeper level what the music meant, what it’s about,” another said. 
“So you really think it’s about metal?” Colter asked. 
They wrestled with the question for a while longer. “This is why you’re not allowed to ask questions,” Nicks told Colter. 
He laughed. “What if I were to say what it’s really about is being human?,” Colter said. “I mean, we’re using a particular lens, right? The lens of a particular kind of music, particular kind of art, particular kind of community. But one of the things that I keep coming back to with all this stuff is how this is just a way of being human, and a way of exploring what it means to each of us to be human.”
From left to right: Sharay Burnett, Taylor Nicks, Amy Doerr, Paulette Iliff, Lorrie Hood and Kelly Turner move their graduation cap tassels at their college graduation ceremony at the Wyoming Women’s Center in Lusk on August 20, 2026. (Maya Shimizu Harris/WyoFile)
Pathways from Prison is set to graduate more students — a group of men from Torrington’s Medium Correctional Institution — next summer. The program received funds to expand to other facilities and support previous graduates in serving as mentors for new students. 
At the Wyoming Women’s Center, students for the new class have already been chosen. They sat in the audience at their peers’ Aug. 20 graduation ceremony. The graduating students’ friends and family members filled the room, which had been decorated with brown and gold flowers, balloons and streamers. A poster behind the podium read: “Congratulations! Class of 2026.” 

Taylor Nicks sits with her son at her college graduation ceremony at the Wyoming Women’s Center in Lusk on August 20, 2026. (Maya Shimizu Harris/WyoFile)

The students, wearing graduation caps and gowns, stood to receive their diplomas from Colter. “I couldn’t be prouder than I am at this moment,” Colter told the gathered people. The students moved their tassels from the right to the left and flung their caps into the air. After the ceremony, Iliff took photos with her best friend. Hood greeted her parents. Nicks embraced her son. 
“When I got arrested, my son was 2, and I’ve been locked up seven years now,” Nicks had said earlier. 
“I made a promise to myself and to God when I got arrested that I wasn’t gonna let this time be wasted. I’m away from my family, and my son’s having to grow up without me, and I didn’t want to not grow from this experience. I wanted to take every opportunity that this place offered me and grow.”

name: WyoFile
title: Roses, Carnations, and a vote that took 50 years
authors: by WyoHistory.org editors Leslie Waggener and Kylie Louise McCormick
description:
Wyoming women laid out a model for nationwide suffrage and didn’t stop lobbying and organizing until their right was secured, write WyoHistory.org editors Leslie Waggener and Kylie McCormick.
The post Roses, Carnations, and a vote that took 50 years appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
On the night of Aug. 18, 1920, the phone rang at Grace Raymond Hebard’s home in Laramie. Tennessee had just become the 36th state to ratify the 19th Amendment, finally securing woman suffrage as the law of the land. Hebard burst into applause, startling the operator on the line, then went out to help ring the bells at Laramie’s Episcopal cathedral.
Hebard, a University of Wyoming professor, had spent the better part of a year lobbying governors and legislators from Wyoming to Connecticut to help bring that night about. Her home state gave her reason to feel entitled to celebrate: Wyoming entered the Union in 1890 as the first state in the nation to guarantee women full, unrestricted voting rights. Statehood wasn’t the end of the story. It was the start of a decades-long argument, carried by Wyoming women onto the national stage, over whether the rest of the country would catch up.
Two years after admission, Wyoming women became the first in the nation to vote in a presidential election. By the 1890s, Colorado, Utah and Idaho had followed Wyoming’s lead. The state’s 1869 suffrage law, passed by a territorial legislature that few outsiders were watching, had become a model other states began to export.
Building the case, nationally
Much of that work happened through organizations, not headlines. In July 1916, the National Council of Women Voters held its third convention in Cheyenne, drawing about 25 Wyoming women and 16 delegates from other states, including Hebard and Mary Godat Bellamy, the state’s first woman legislator. The convention voted to affiliate with the National American Woman Suffrage Association, or NAWSA, then the country’s dominant suffrage organization.
That affiliation put Wyoming inside the machinery of the national fight. Congress passed the 19th Amendment in June 1919, requiring ratification by 36 of the 48 states, and suffragists nationwide began a coordinated push to get there.
Hebard and the ratification fight
Wyoming’s role in that push centered on Hebard herself. Born in 1861 in Clinton, Iowa, she earned a Bachelor of Science in civil engineering from the University of Iowa in 1882, then worked in Cheyenne as a draftsman before a brief, unhappy stint as deputy state engineer. She found a better opportunity at the newly opened University of Wyoming in Laramie, where she built a four-decade career, and she stayed close with her Iowa classmate Carrie Chapman Catt throughout.
Late in 1919, Wyoming suffragists formed a 26-person ratification committee led by Hebard. On Nov. 11, 1919, Catt, by then NAWSA’s nationally prominent president, met with the committee in Laramie as part of a final lobbying push. The committee’s task: Persuade Gov. Robert D. Carey to call a special session of the Legislature, because Wyoming’s regular session wouldn’t meet again in time to make the ratification deadline. Fellow committee member Theresa Jenkins, a well-known Wyoming suffragist and temperance orator, appealed to Carey directly. Carey’s answer, as Jenkins later recounted it, was personal: “Mrs. Jenkins, if for no other reason than that you have asked me to do this I would call this session, for I know that if you did not think it the right thing for me to do you would not have asked it.”
Carey called the session. The Legislature convened Jan. 26-28, 1920. When the Senate ratified unanimously on the first day, Hebard marked the occasion by presenting each senator with a rose; the House followed a day later and got carnations instead. Carey signed the resolution Jan. 28, making Wyoming the 27th of the 36 states needed.
By late March 1920, two-thirds of the states had ratified the amendment. Suffragists hoped Connecticut Gov. Marcus H. Holcomb would provide the final vote needed, and Catt recruited Hebard for the Suffrage Emergency Corps to press him. In Connecticut, Hebard made her case by pointing at her own record: “I am not making a plea for myself. I have voted for 38 years. What man in the audience has for 38 consecutive years voted for every state, county and municipal election, and during 10 years of that time traveled 104 miles every time he voted?” Despite the pressure, Holcomb, a staunch anti-suffragist, refused to budge. It took five more months, and a narrow vote in Tennessee, to finally put the amendment over the top. .
Carrie Chapman Catt, center, at a gathering in celebration of her honorary degree from the University of Wyoming, 1921. (UW American Heritage Center)
The limits of “every woman”
Yet the claim to equal voting rights was broader than the reality. Wyoming’s 1869 law required voters to be citizens or swear intent to become one — a bar that excluded Native American women, who were not recognized as U.S. citizens, and Chinese immigrant women, barred from naturalization under federal law. The 19th Amendment didn’t fix that gap. Native American women didn’t gain citizenship until the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924, and many states continued to bar Native voters through other means for decades after.
A wave of firsts
With the amendment ratified, Wyoming women kept adding to the state’s list of national firsts, some of them almost immediately.
Dayton elected Susan Wissler mayor in 1912, Wyoming’s first woman to hold the office. Jackson went further in 1920, voting in an all-woman town council that the national press nicknamed the “petticoat government.”
The biggest first was still to come. In 1924, a month after her husband, Gov. William B. Ross, died in office, Nellie Tayloe Ross was elected to succeed him. She took the oath Jan. 5, 1925 — the first woman governor in U.S. history.
Other firsts took longer to arrive. Women had briefly served on Wyoming juries in 1870, but that right had to be rebuilt from scratch: Not until 1950 did Louise Spinner Graf serve as foreman of a jury in Green River, the first in the state to include women in eight decades. Verda James, a schoolteacher in Casper, reached the Wyoming House in 1954 and served eight terms.
Then, in 1980, Cheyenne schoolteacher Harriett Elizabeth “Liz” Byrd became the first Black woman elected to the Wyoming Legislature. For nearly a decade there, she fought for one thing: a state holiday honoring Martin Luther King Jr. Nine times she introduced the bill. In 1990, it finally passed, as Martin Luther King Jr./Wyoming Equality Day.
Thyra Thomson and the Equal Rights Amendment
By the early 1970s, Wyoming’s highest-ranking elected woman was Secretary of State Thyra Thomson, in office for 24 years. When Congress passed the Equal Rights Amendment in 1972, Thomson used her position to lobby for it.





Click to enlarge: Thyra Thomson at the Cody Stampede in July 1980. (UW American Heritage Center).

She didn’t have to make the case from scratch. The Legislature’s own Commission on the Status of Women had already made it in a 1972 report that didn’t soften the finding: “although our state is known as the ‘Equality State’…sex discrimination does exist and, in many cases, is accepted as normal.”
The Equal Rights Amendment vote that followed was closer than the state’s suffrage history might suggest, and the opposition wasn’t simply men against women: Many letters against ratification came from women who said they already had all the rights they wanted. The Wyoming House ratified 40 to 21 on Jan. 16, 1973. The Senate was the real fight, ratifying 17 to 12 on Jan. 24, making Wyoming the 23rd state to approve the amendment. Behind that vote stood a coalition of women’s organizations led by Selia Ribeiro and Julia Yelvington, backed publicly by both Gov. Stan Hathaway and Thomson herself.
The following year, only seven of the Legislature’s 92 members were women, six in the House and one in the Senate. Thomson said as much at a Casper Women’s Conference banquet that December: Wyoming’s early advances hadn’t finished the job. Federal equality laws were poorly enforced, and some state laws written to protect women had instead boxed them out.
Thomson kept making that case for the rest of her career. At a Cheyenne Equal Rights Amendment rally in 1981, she distilled it to one line: “All human beings must be equal and free. Love is liberation.” She was just as blunt about what hadn’t changed: Wyoming had never passed equal-pay legislation, a gap she said gave the Equality State a “black eye.” Testifying before a legislative committee in 1985, she cited women earning 54 cents for every dollar paid to men and dismissed cost objections outright: “Cost was the argument used against doing away with child labor and slavery.”
Where Wyoming stands now
The numbers suggest that the state’s early momentum didn’t carry as far as its reputation. In 1985, women held 24 of Wyoming’s 94 state legislative seats — a share that still ranked third in the nation. Four decades later, the number of seats held by women is almost unchanged — 24 of 93 in 2026 — but other states have gained ground, dropping Wyoming’s national rank to 41st.
The pay gap Thomson cited in 1985 has also outlasted her. Wyoming law has barred gender-based wage discrimination since an 1869 equal-pay statute for teachers, but Wyoming still has one of the largest gender pay gaps in the country. The pattern holds all the way to the top: The state hasn’t elected a second woman governor since Ross left office a century ago; its “first” has had no second.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Crews finishing new wildlife crossing in southeast Idaho to protect migrating deer
description: Crews are nearing completion of a new wildlife underpass in southeast Idaho after the public, nonprofit agencies, conservation groups and government agencies pushed for years to protect migrating wildlife herds and drivers. The Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass is expected to be completed this fall along U.S. Highway 30, south of Montpelier in Bear Lake County,[...]
text:
Crews are completing the new Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass south of Montpelier in Bear Lake County. (Photo by Julia Barton/Greater Yellowstone Coalition)Crews are nearing completion of a new wildlife underpass in southeast Idaho after the public, nonprofit agencies, conservation groups and government agencies pushed for years to protect migrating wildlife herds and drivers.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass is expected to be completed this fall along U.S. Highway 30, south of Montpelier in Bear Lake County, public officials and conservationists announced jointly this week. 
The wildlife crossing features three underpasses, as well as extensive fencing on either side of the project to direct animals like deer to the wildlife crossing. 
“We were seeing just all kinds of problems there; we were losing at least 100 deer a year,” Idaho Transportation Department public information officer Justin Smith said in an interview Wednesday. “Over 10 years, that is 1,000 animals we know we lost.”
Officials also said those collisions cost drivers and taxpayers millions of dollars every year.
“Our primary concern is the safety of the traveling public. Whether they are going through a construction zone or whether they are in a wildlife area, we want to keep people safe on our highways, and this is part of that effort,” Smith said.
The Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass represents a partnership between the Idaho Transportation Department, Idaho Department of Fish and Game, the Greater Yellowstone Coalition, the Idaho Conservation League and Bear Lake County, officials said. 
This map depicts the project area for the Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass near Montpelier. (Map courtesy of Greater Yellowstone Coalition)
“Rocky Point shows what’s possible when agencies, conservation and sporting groups and local communities work toward the same goal,” Matt Lucia, Idaho conservation manager at the Greater Yellowstone Coalition, said in a written statement. “(The Greater Yellowstone Coalition) has been part of this project for years — contributing time, energy and funds toward the effort. The next step is making sure the federal funding that made this project possible stays available.”
To build the crossing, the Idaho Transportation Department secured a $20.8 million grant from the Federal Highway Administration’s Wildlife Crossing Pilot Program. Funding comes from the federal Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act that was passed by Congress and signed into law by former President Joe Biden in 2021.  
The federal grant was estimated to cover 98% of the construction costs, but the project may come in under budget, allowing the state to return some of the money to the Federal Highway Administration, Smith said.
 Idaho’s first major highway wildlife crossing was built outside of Boise in 2023

Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



The Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass near Montpelier is the second major wildlife highway crossing in Idaho. 
In 2023, crews built the Cervidae Peak Wildlife Overpass on Idaho Highway 21 near Lucky Peak, between Boise and Idaho City. 
The Cervidae overpass features more than one mile of big game fencing to direct the animals to the safe crossing. 
Fish and Game officials installed a wildlife camera at the crossing to document how it is working. In 2024, state officials posted a time-lapse video showing more than 1,000 deer safely using the Cervidae Peak Wildlife Overpass between Oct. 17, 2024, and Dec. 18, 2024. 

Smith said officials with the Idaho Transportation Department are studying other highway corridors with heavy wildlife populations, and the state is open to pursuing other new wildlife crossings as well. 
“It is something that as Idaho’s population continues to grow, we need to look at ways to protect drivers and protect the wildlife,” Smith said. “It’s something we continue to look at.”
“We’re always open to doing what needs to be done for the safety of the traveling public; that is our primary concern,” Smith added. “We will continue to look at these projects as ways to improve the safety on our highways.”
The Idaho Legislature has also called for more wildlife crossings. In March, the Idaho Legislature adopted Senate Concurrent Resolution 124. 
The resolution encourages the Idaho Legislature, Idaho’s congressional delegation, the governor, the Idaho Transportation Department and Fish and Game to recognize and support wildlife corridors to improve public safety and protect big game migration corridors. 
“The Legislature strongly supports the advancement of public safety and conservation of Idaho’s big game migration corridors through the development and implementation of wildlife crossings where appropriate and supported by local communities,” the resolution states.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama state library board creates sample policies to implement controversial rule changes
description: The Alabama Public Library Service unveiled a set of sample policies earlier this summer that they say will allow local libraries to remain in compliance with controversial administrative code changes adopted in the past two years. The set includes three examples, known as A, B and C, with different formats, but all contain the elements […]
text:
Books on display in the teen section of the Fairhope Public Library on March 2, 2026. The APLS created sample policies for local libraries to use that align with the recent changes to the administrative code. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama Public Library Service unveiled a set of sample policies earlier this summer that they say will allow local libraries to remain in compliance with controversial administrative code changes adopted in the past two years.
The set includes three examples, known as A, B and C, with different formats, but all contain the elements of changes approved by APLS in 2024 and 2025 that directed local libraries to restrict content or risk losing state aid.
“We wanted to make sure they had examples that they could use,” said John Wahl, chair of the APLS Board and Republican nominee for lieutenant governor, in an interview Thursday. “Nothing that was required, just ideas where they could take them to their local boards, make any edits they wanted to make and streamline their process, especially for libraries that didn’t have someone to draft policies for themselves.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In 2024, board members ratified updates that required libraries to create policies restricting minors’ access to  materials that are considered obscene, sexually explicit “or otherwise inappropriate.”
In 2025, members of the APLS Board updated the administrative code for a second time to prohibit library materials that dealt with gender ideology, but without defining the term.
“In the past we would have policy requirements that were much more broad and open, and allowed for individual library boards to tailor those policies to the specific needs of their communities,” said Mary Campbell, president of the Alabama Library Association. “These do not allow you to do that.”
The changes came after right-wing activists targeted libraries in Alabama and around the nation, claiming youth sections of libraries contained explicit or sexually suggestive materials. Some of the books targeted used inclusive pronouns, and critics said the books were being targeted for having LGBTQ+ themes or characters.
Read Freely Alabama, a group that organized to oppose the changes, criticized Wahl and board member Amy Minton in a statement, saying the policies “make clear that this was never about protecting children from explicit content.”
“Libraries are being compelled to treat books about transgender people and gender identity as inherently ‘sexually explicit,’ a vague term that seems to change to reflect whatever John Wahl and Amy Minton want it to regardless of actual sexual content,” the statement said.
Thus far, the Fairhope Public Library has been the lone library to forfeit state aid for refusing to move specific materials that the APLS board objected to.
Example policies have the same statement that bans discrimination, but with an added caveat to accommodate the administrative code changes.
“Exercising discretion in the location of sexually explicit material or other material deemed by the public library board to be inappropriate for children or youth does not constitute a denial of service on the basis of age,” the policies state. “Taking age into account when recommending, displaying or otherwise actively promoting library materials does not constitute a denial of service on the basis of age.”
The sample policies differ in their specificity. But all include sections that refer to specific elements within the administrative code and provide justification.
“Different libraries have different structures with their bylaws for the codes, and we wanted them to have options that fit well with the structure of their local protocols,” Wahl said.
The main changes that board members imposed on the administrative code dealt with library collections and reshelving materials, library cards, displays for content and membership with the American Library Association.
Example A appeared to be the least specific. The selection criteria section had bullet points for relevance, quality and demand, along with a statement that “These criteria safeguard minors from sexually explicit or other material deemed by the public library board to be inappropriate for children or youth.”
The section to reshelve library materials outlined the same criteria that restricted minors from having access to specific library materials and had a statement regarding the gender ideology ban.
“Under this rule, any materials regarding transgender procedures, gender ideology, or the concept of more than two biological genders shall be considered inappropriate for children and youth,” the example policy states.
Example C included more details. It had a section titled “Application and Purpose” that referred to “protecting minors from obscene, sexually explicit, or other material deemed by the public library board to be inappropriate for children or youth.”
The section for selection materials had a numbered list of rules that largely aligned with the paragraphs in Example A but had other particulars.
“All materials intended for minors must be reviewed and approved by designated library staff,” the policy states.
The physical location section in Example C laid out criteria for filing complaints related to library materials.
“Citizens may, upon furnishing proof of residency, initiate a Request of Reconsideration of any library material by filling out the applicable form,” the example policy states. “Requests for Reconsideration are reviewed according to established criteria and procedures, guaranteeing transparency in the decision-making and ensuring that every citizen has a voice in the process.”
Campbell said that the sample policies could help smaller and more rural libraries without adequate staffing to develop policies aligning with the administrative code. But she said it will not solve other issues.
“One of the main issues is the subjectiveness of some of some of the requirements, like what is ‘inappropriate for children,’” Campbell said.
The set of sample policies is one approach that APLS staff have tried to address issues that local libraries face to comply with the administrative code changes.
APLS Director Kelyn Ralya is still considering whether to fill a post that was created to coordinate with local libraries to comply with the administrative code changes. That decision remains pending.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee slightly sheds jobs for 8th month in row, inflation at 3.4%
description: The state’s top economic advisor at the University of Tennessee isn’t concerned yet, even as job numbers show that, for the eighth month in a row, the number of people employed in the state has slightly dropped.  Tennessee’s economy has experienced year-over-year job growth since an initial spike in unemployment at the start of the […]
text:
Tennessee shed jobs for the eighth month in a row, according to federal data. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The state’s top economic advisor at the University of Tennessee isn’t concerned yet, even as job numbers show that, for the eighth month in a row, the number of people employed in the state has slightly dropped. 
Tennessee’s economy has experienced year-over-year job growth since an initial spike in unemployment at the start of the coronavirus pandemic. Then in 2022, the state experienced a few months of job losses, but still managed to add more jobs over the course of the year. 
But the latest economic data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics show that from December 2025 to July 2026, roughly 55,000 fewer Tennesseans have jobs. More than 3.42 million Tennesseans were employed in November 2025, and as of July, that number was 3.37 million. 


Don Bruce, a professor with the University of Tennessee’s Boyd Center for Business and Economic Research, said that the short-term drop in employment numbers is not something he’s concerned about until it becomes a multi-year trend.
“We are still above where we were pre-pandemic,” Bruce said. “I’m comfortable that our state economy is strong enough to weather short-term fluctuations in employment.”
TN unemployment low, but sheds jobs for the 5th month in a row

Despite shedding jobs, Tennessee’s unemployment rate fell in July to 3.4%. Outside the early pandemic months, Tennessee’s unemployment rate has remained below 4% since April 2017. 
Tennessee’s unemployment rate still remains low because fewer people are working. Economists at the University of Tennessee have attributed this to a steady increase in retirements, the rise of artificial intelligence and recent crackdowns on immigrant workers. 
The other economic concern for state officials is inflation, which sits at about 3.4%. Typically, the U.S. Federal Reserve targets a yearly inflation rate of 2%.
Bruce said oil prices are driving inflation, which makes it less likely that the U.S. Federal Reserve will cut interest rates this year. The increase in oil prices reverberates throughout the economy, making almost every shipped product more expensive. 
The price of oil spiked dramatically in February after President Donald Trump launched a war with Iran. Prices have fluctuated more widely over the past six months because of the war, and remain higher today than at any point in 2025.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat

title: Summit forfeits two CO2 storage permits in North Dakota, continues legal fight over third
description: Summit Carbon Solutions is abandoning two-thirds of its planned project to store carbon dioxide underground in North Dakota.  The company, which had been granted permits to store CO2 in three designated areas in central North Dakota, has requested permits for two of the areas to be canceled.  “Summit #1 and Summit #2 have determined as […]
text:
Summit Carbon Solutions representatives pictured at an event in Sioux Falls in January, 2025. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)Summit Carbon Solutions is abandoning two-thirds of its planned project to store carbon dioxide underground in North Dakota. 
The company, which had been granted permits to store CO2 in three designated areas in central North Dakota, has requested permits for two of the areas to be canceled. 
“Summit #1 and Summit #2 have determined as a matter of business judgment that they will not proceed with development, construction, operation, or implementation of either proposed storage facility,” Summit said in a filing with the North Dakota Supreme Court. 
A North Dakota district court voided permits for all three areas earlier this year. Summit and the state are appealing that decision. But the company is now asking the Supreme Court to limit the appeal to one of the storage areas, known as Summit #3. 
The company’s decision to abandon two of its storage facility permits is a victory for many of the landowners opposing the project. Most of those landowners have objected to what they characterize as the company’s unwillingness to negotiate on matters of liability and compensation. Only one of the landowners involved in the litigation owns property in the third storage area. 
Courts order North Dakota to pay landowners’ legal fees in two lawsuits

In an email last week, Summit said it is prioritizing Summit #3, where the company has about 98% of the storage rights secured.
Summit’s filing stated the Industrial Commission, a three-member board chaired by Gov. Kelly Armstrong that regulates CO2 storage among other things, had approved the two permit cancellations. 
The company’s original proposal involved transporting carbon dioxide from ethanol plants in five states to central North Dakota where it could be injected into rock layers deep underground. The injection sites were located at the intersection of Mercer, McLean and Oliver counties. 
Summit announced a change of plans earlier this year. The company now plans to transport carbon dioxide to a storage site in Wyoming for injection underground, but did not close the door on continuing to pursue its North Dakota operations to some degree. 
Summit said in an email that its North Dakota pipeline route easements and storage rights are still valuable assets.
“Over time, we expect to further develop and utilize these assets as opportunities materialize,” the statement said. 
The company’s storage permits from the Industrial Commission, the state law authorizing the Industrial Commission to issue those permits, and the pipeline route permit from the Public Service Commission are all the subject of litigation in North Dakota. District court judges have voided the storage permits and struck down the underlying law; both cases are on appeal to the Supreme Court. The third case is waiting on a decision from the district court.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.

text:
Thursday’s ruling, which was backed by two of former President Donald Trump’s nominees to the bench, marked the third major legal challenge of the 2010 law to fail at the nation’s highest court.
At stake was the health care coverage of more than 21 million people nationally who have gained insurance through the marketplace. (Getty Images)
Last week, a pair of Democratic lawmakers from the Michigan House and Senate shared that they were working on legislation to ensure more Michigan residents can access healthcare. 
State Rep. Mai Xiong (D-Warren) and state Sen. John Cherry (D-Flint) on Wednesday announced that they had each introduced legislation to create a Medicaid buy-in program, with Xiong introducing House Bill 6274 and Cherry introducing Senate Bill 1152. 
If the bills are signed into law, Michiganders earning between 133% and 200% of the federal poverty level who do not qualify for Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program would have access to health benefits at a lower premium that what they would pay through a qualified health plan purchased through the Affordable Care Act’s Health Insurance Marketplace. 
State Rep. Mai Xiong (D-Warren) on the House floor on May 1, 2025. | Kyle DavidsonState Sen. John Cherry (D-Flint) speaks in support of bills to repeal Right to Work laws, March 14, 2023 | Laina G. Stebbins
“Health premiums are skyrocketing and too often workers on the frontlines of the construction, food service and home care industries are forced to budget out the largest percentage of their paycheck just to keep their families covered,” Xiong said in a statement. “Our legislation gives hardworking Michiganders who don’t qualify for public healthcare assistance programs an affordable option. No matter what job or industry someone works in or income level, they deserve access to healthcare.”
New York, Oregon, Minnesota and Washington D.C. have already adopted similar legislation making use of an option in the Affordable Care Act allowing states to create a basic health program. The program covers both citizens and lawfully present noncitizens.
“Michiganders are already stretched thin with ever-increasing costs,” Cherry said. “Our constituents should never have to choose between keeping food on the table or seeking care. With the introduction of this legislation, we take an important step toward reducing healthcare costs for those individuals stuck at wit’s end in the marketplace.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Flock tracks your license plate. We tracked the $2M it spent on lobbying.
description: Flock Safety has poured more than $2 million into federal and state lobbying since 2025 as the fast‑growing surveillance company faces mounting scrutiny from lawmakers in both parties and privacy advocates over its ever-expanding network of license‑plate‑tracking cameras. The company spent nearly $1.3 million between January 2025 and July 2026 on federal lob[...]
text:
A Flock camera on the corner of La Harpe Boulevard and North Chester Street in Little Rock on Aug. 19, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate) 

Flock Safety has poured more than $2 million into federal and state lobbying since 2025 as the fast‑growing surveillance company faces mounting scrutiny from lawmakers in both parties and privacy advocates over its ever-expanding network of license‑plate‑tracking cameras.


The company spent nearly $1.3 million between January 2025 and July 2026 on federal lobbying and at least another $1 million in statehouses across the U.S., according to OpenSecrets’ federal lobbying data and an analysis of lobbying disclosures across all 50 states. Flock has hired lobbyists in dozens of states – often former government employees passing through the political “revolving door” – including in places where weak disclosure laws mean spending totals are not publicly reported.
Flock has drawn increasing criticism over the vast, largely unregulated network of automated cameras it operates nationwide. The cameras record license plate numbers and other characteristics of all vehicles passing by, allowing thousands of law enforcement agencies in 49 states (all except Alaska) to search and share Flock’s data across jurisdictions. This enables police to track vehicles in real time and build investigative dossiers from billions of scans collected each month.
Several Arkansas cities pull plug on Flock cameras

While police agencies praise the system as a tool for locating missing people and tracking suspects, privacy advocates warn the technology enables mass surveillance without a warrant. And amid a nationwide wave of protests and vandalism targeting the company’s cameras, more than 120 agencies or jurisdictions have canceled, suspended or rejected a contract – or deactivated their cameras – since January 2025, according to a tracker maintained by DeFlock, a group that opposes their use.
Many of those terminations followed concerns raised about improper data access, including instances in which officers conducted personal searches – raising a central question: What, exactly, does Flock want from this lobbying push? OpenSecrets reached out to the company for comment but did not receive a response.
Torin Monahan, a professor at the University of North Carolina and co-editor of the peer-reviewed journal Surveillance & Society, identified several likely items on Flock’s lobbying agenda. He said the company is likely focused on securing long-term contracts with municipalities and counties as well as avoiding potential restrictions that could require police to obtain a warrant before using the system or limit the cross-jurisdiction data sharing that underpins Flock’s network.
“Some of the things they’re lobbying for are things that they’re worried about,” Monahan told OpenSecrets. “I would imagine those are areas where they would like to head those restrictions off at the pass, if they could.”
He also suggested that Flock “wants to become the monopoly for this particular service” of license plate readers because the network gains power as the user count grows.
Flock says it has deals with more than 5,000 law enforcement agencies across 6,000 communities. The company leases its cameras to governments, private neighborhoods and other groups, typically charging an annual fee of $2,500 to $3,000 per camera.
“So if you have more adoption throughout the country, then it probably will … barring any political blowback, persuade other clients that this is the right company that they should contract with for these services,” Monahan said.
Flock’s federal lobbying spending nears $1.4M
Flock is coming off its highest-spending quarter since it began lobbying the federal government in 2024. Between April 1 and June 30, 2026, the company reported $220,000 in federal lobbying spending after spending $210,000 in each of the five preceding quarters.
In total, it has spent nearly $1.4 million on federal lobbying, including $840,000 in 2025 and $430,000 so far in 2026.
While the company has not reported lobbying on specific bills, its 2026 filings show activity focused on both chambers of Congress and the White House, including the Office of Administration. Its lobbyists have been working on broad issue areas including homeland security, law enforcement, crime and criminal justice – an agenda that aligns with the company’s efforts to expand its camera network.
Several of Flock’s competitors also are active on K Street, though those legacy firms operate far larger product portfolios.
Axon Enterprise, a weapons and tech company formerly known as Taser, has spent nearly $5.3 million on federal lobbying since 2024 on a range of issues topped by homeland security, law enforcement, crime and criminal justice. Motorola Solutions – the parent of surveillance vendor Vigilant Solutions – has spent about $5 million in the same time frame, with its most frequently cited issues including the federal budget and appropriations, telecommunications, defense and intelligence. But the lobbying activity by those companies is not broken out by subsidiary or product line, making it unclear how much of their spending is tied specifically to automated license plate reader systems.
Much of Flock’s lobbying work has been handled by veterans of the revolving door – former public servants now advocating on its behalf. Five of the seven lobbyists hired by Flock this year fall into that category.
Among them: Bryan Lanza of Mercury Public Affairs, who served as communications director for President Donald Trump’s first transition team; Jennifer Lawkin Lukawski of BGR Group, the first executive director of the Republican Study Committee in the House of Representatives; and BGR Group President Erskine Wells, a former deputy chief of staff for Sen. Roger Wicker (R‑Miss.).
Flock lobbying in statehouses with mixed disclosure requirements
An OpenSecrets review of all 50 state lobbying disclosure databases showed Flock with active lobbyists in 34 states in 2025 and/or 2026. Those filings documented at least $1 million in state-level lobbying during that span – but that figure almost certainly understates the company’s true spending because many states do not require lobbyists or their clients to report compensation.
In 18 of those states, Flock’s lobbyists were active but no spending totals were available. State disclosure laws vary widely, from detailed quarterly reports to systems that exclude retainer fees entirely, and those gaps in reporting requirements create blind spots in understanding the company’s full financial footprint.
In Arizona, for example, Flock retained Molera Alvarez – a prominent Phoenix lobbying firm co-founded by a former state superintendent of schools and staffed with several former state and municipal government employees – to represent its interests in 2025. Yet the state’s lobbying database shows no reportable expenditures. Arizona law excludes lobbyist compensation and retainer fees from disclosure. The secretary of state’s summary of principal expenditures from the previous year also lists $0.
Similarly, in Alabama, the company hired former Secretary of State Beth Chapman in 2025 to lobby state officials. But Flock’s quarterly disclosure forms list $0 in reportable spending, consistent with state ethics rules that do not require companies to disclose private retainer fees.
Flock’s largest known expenditure came in California, where since January 2025 it spent $30,000 in each quarter for a total of $180,000. The company focused its efforts on bills adding guardrails around vendor contracts for license plate reader systems – including measures requiring data that fails to produce a hit to be purged within 30 days, mandating audits, requiring case numbers for queries and blocking cross-agency sharing without authorization.
Of those six bills, only one passed both chambers. That bill would have established data protection requirements for license-plate-reader systems, but Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) vetoed it in September 2025. The others died in committee or stalled in the appropriations process.
“I view the lobbying money … in the same category of trying to influence in advance what the particular outcomes might be,” Monahan said.
Flock also spent $169,000 since January 2025 on lobbying in Massachusetts on issues related to police, fire and law enforcement organizations, and $102,000 in Wisconsin lobbying on state Senate and Assembly bills to establish grants for law enforcement agencies to purchase license-plate-reader systems. In Tennessee, where lobbying disclosures include ranges instead of specific spending amounts, Flock paid its lobbying team between $25,000 and $50,000 in both 2025 and 2026 while recording less than $10,000 in expenses in both years.
By comparison, Flock’s contracts with municipalities and universities routinely climb into the hundreds of thousands of dollars. Monahan noted that some universities pay $750,000 to lease Flock’s systems and city and county deployments can top $1 million.
“It seems like a drop in the bucket compared to the size of their contracts,” Monahan said.
In a sign of its expanding lobbying footprint, Flock registered a lobbyist in Wyoming on June 29.
Minimal spending on campaigns by Flock leaders
Compared to Flock’s lobbying spending, the political activity by its leadership is scant.
Corporations are prohibited from donating directly to candidates or political action committees. Flock Safety does not operate a political action committee for its employees to contribute to, and there is no record of any independent expenditure committee – or, a super PAC – funded by the company or its executives. Nor is there any record of the company or its leaders donating to Trump’s inaugural fund, a legal loophole that allows corporations to give unlimited sums.
OpenSecrets data shows CEO Garrett Langley donated $1,000 in 2024 to Health Jobs Justice, the leadership PAC for Sen. Jon Ossoff (D‑Ga.). Beyond that single contribution, there is no visible federal political giving from Flock’s top executives.
Beyond lobbying: The data question
But Flock’s ambitions extend beyond shaping policy. Monahan said the company is diversifying its portfolio beyond license-plate readers and adding drones, gunfire location systems and citywide “safety dashboards” that aggregate public data.
Taken together, it’s a sign that “the law enforcement space is getting pretty crowded” and that mounting scrutiny may be pushing the company to expand, Monahan said.
But that expansion raises questions that go beyond lobbying dollars, because Monahan said the data Flock collects isn’t used just for law enforcement purposes. It also trains the company’s proprietary AI models.
“What we don’t know, as the public, is where all those data are going. How might compromising data be included in these models? What controls might we have about the applications that these AI systems are being put toward?” he said.
Those are questions, Monahan said, that Flock’s lobbying disclosures don’t answer – and that neither regulators nor the municipalities signing contracts with the company have yet to seriously ask.


This article was originally published by OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization that tracks money in politics.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: ICE released man formerly detained in Aurora without his ID in unfamiliar state
description: Rudy Villeda Mejía, who spent just over four months in immigration detention in Aurora, is home with his family in northern Washington state.  His journey home was drawn out, as his family and attorney struggled to locate him when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement released him in a state more than 2,000 miles from home […]
text:
Rudy Villeda Mejía runs a roofing business in northern Washington that has struggled since U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested him in March. (Photo courtesy of Mabel Shaffer)Rudy Villeda Mejía, who spent just over four months in immigration detention in Aurora, is home with his family in northern Washington state. 
His journey home was drawn out, as his family and attorney struggled to locate him when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement released him in a state more than 2,000 miles from home after the agency nearly deported him.
A judge ordered on Aug. 3 that ICE release Villeda Mejía, 47, from detention because he has a pending application for a T visa, which is designated for victims of human trafficking. That makes him part of a protected class under a May court order from California that blocked ICE from detaining immigrants with pending T visa applications, along with other visas for crime victims. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Villeda Mejía is adjusting after his return home and is back to work at his roofing business, which suffered financial losses while Villeda Mejía was detained, struggling to repay debts for new equipment the company purchased. 
“Now he’s just trying to catch up with work,” Genaro Shaffer, Villeda Mejía’s stepson, said. “We have all these roofs that we’re doing, and he’s just constantly working, working, working every day. It’s got to be exhausting after going straight from detention to work.”
Villeda Mejía, originally from Honduras, has lived in the U.S. since he entered without authorization in 2010, when he was kidnapped by a violent cartel in Mexico that brought him over the border, according to a notarized personal statement Villeda Mejía submitted with his visa application. 
​He fled gang violence. Now this ICE detainee in Aurora tries to avoid deportation.

ICE arrested Villeda Mejía at Denver International Airport on March 30. He was detained at the ICE detention center in Aurora until early August, when ICE moved him across the country to a “staging facility” in Louisiana — the final stop before ICE deports someone, according to Henry Hollithron, Villeda Mejía’s Denver-based attorney. 
Shortly after he arrived in Louisiana, Judge Regina Rodriguez of U.S. District Court in Colorado ordered his release. Her order prohibits ICE from re-detaining Villeda Mejía unless it demonstrates at a hearing that he is a flight risk or danger to the community. 
Stripped of passport
Villeda Mejía’s wife flew to Louisiana, where the couple rented a car to drive back to Washington, according to Shaffer. That was only after the family and Hollithron scrambled to narrow down exactly where ICE released Villeda Mejía.
ICE told one family member he was still in Aurora. Another person detained in Aurora told a different family member he was no longer in Aurora. Hollithron’s office heard he was in Oakdale, Louisiana. Then that changed to Alexandria, Louisiana, and again to Winnfield, Louisiana. 
“We’re sure he’s in Louisiana somewhere. We just don’t know where in Louisiana he actually is, because the left hand doesn’t know what the right hand is doing,” Hollithron said. “This is the reality of families dealing with immigration detention. You can’t even find your relatives half the time.”
Shaffer said he ultimately learned that ICE flew Villeda Mejía to Arizona and then to Texas, and he was driven from Texas to Louisiana. 



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



ICE has arrested and deported thousands of immigrants across the U.S. since President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025 as part of his mass deportation scheme, which ensnares immigrants who lack permanent legal status. While the Trump administration has said those efforts target criminals, many of those arrested do not have criminal records, only civil immigration violations.
The latest hurdle was getting back Villeda Mejía’s passport and work permit, which remained in Colorado after ICE transported him to Louisiana. Without an ID, Villeda Mejía couldn’t fly home from Louisiana, Hollithron said, and even if he had his ID, his family feared that ICE would attempt to detain him at the airport again. 
ICE’s Denver Field Office declined to answer Newsline’s questions about Villeda Mejía’s transport out of Colorado, plans for his deportation or its retention of his personal documents. 



Quotation







This is the reality of families dealing with immigration detention. You can't even find your relatives half the time.


– Henry Hollithron, immigration attorney


Shaffer said Villeda Mejía has now received back his passport and work permit with support from U.S. Rep. Rick Larsen’s office. Larsen is a Democrat who represents the district in Washington where Villeda Mejía’s family lives. 
“My office stands ready to help people detained by ICE access legal services and help loved ones locate their family members in ICE custody,” Larsen said in a statement, which included a link to his visas and immigration page. “After an individual or their family member fills out a privacy release form, my staff can advocate on their behalf to federal agencies like ICE and (U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services).”
‘Imagine the worst day of your life’
While the immediate legal hurdles have ceased, Shaffer said his stepfather is now regaining strength after months in detention led to new difficulties with back pain. Hollithron said some of Villeda Mejía’s Bell’s palsy symptoms also flared up after he didn’t receive medication while detained. Shaffer said Villeda Mejía’s hair has started to turn gray, too.
“The conditions that he lived in were like, imagine the worst day of your life, and then imagine living that … for 120 days straight,” Shaffer said. “Worst sleep, worst food, people threatening to beat you up, it’s horrible.”
He said what his family has gone through with ICE can happen to anyone. 
“Rudy had perfect records, like, you couldn’t be more clean,” Shaffer said. Villeda Mejía attended every check-in scheduled at the Seattle Field Office until he was detained this spring.
Shaffer said hiring a good lawyer and asking members of Congress for help are the best ways to get movement from ICE. 
“ICE will do everything against you possible unless they are personally liable for their actions,” Shaffer said. “The only thing that matters to them is a (judge’s) order.”
