name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio Supreme Court rejects judge’s claim abortion amendment hinders job
description: The Ohio Supreme Court dismissed an Ohio judge’s claim that the reproductive rights amendment in the state constitution hindered him from doing his job. Trumbull County Court of Common Pleas Judge David Engler was elected to the county court’s domestic relations and juvenile division in 2024. He argued to the state supreme court in an […]
text:
The Gavel outside the Supreme Court of the State of Ohio, September 20, 2023, at 65 S. Front Street, Columbus, Ohio. (Photo by Graham Stokes for Ohio Capital Journal. Republish photo only with original article.)The Ohio Supreme Court dismissed an Ohio judge’s claim that the reproductive rights amendment in the state constitution hindered him from doing his job.
Trumbull County Court of Common Pleas Judge David Engler was elected to the county court’s domestic relations and juvenile division in 2024. He argued to the state supreme court in an April filing that the constitutional amendment “is being applied to eliminate parental-consent requirements for minors and to render judicial-bypass proceedings unnecessary or unavailable.”
Going further in his court filing, he argued that voters were “not informed” that the constitutional amendment would “eliminate” judicial bypass proceedings.
Judicial bypass is a longstanding legal method minors can use to ask a judge to allow an abortion without the need for parental permission. In judicial bypass cases, judges assess the “maturity and voluntariness” of a request via hearings and testimony, according to documents related to Engler’s court filing.
“The omission (of the judicial bypass proceedings) concealed a consequence essential to both advocates and opponents, and prevented average voters from understanding that the measure would alter the judiciary’s structure,” Engler wrote to the court.
The judge asked the court to dictate the administration and enforcement of the amendment “in a manner that preserves and does not eliminate or interfere with juvenile-court jurisdiction over judicial-bypass proceedings.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.Judicial bypass has been a method since the late 1990s. Engler’s county of Trumbull only saw two judicial bypass requests per year in the five years before he took the bench. In the year since he took over as judge, that number dropped to zero, leading Engler to say his office “has been stripped of a statutory and historically exercised judicial function.”
The reproductive rights amendment was passed by 57% of Ohio voters in 2023, enshrining abortion rights, miscarriage treatment, and other reproductive health measures into the state’s founding document.
The judge’s claims were countered by groups like the ACLU of Ohio and the Reproductive Rights Law Initiative at Case Western Reserve School of Law, along with the Ohio Attorney General’s Office.
Requesting that the court dismiss Engler’s claims, the state attorney general’s office called Engler’s arguments “untimely.” The office and the organizations who filed court documents in opposition to Engler’s request said he did not provide evidence that the constitutional amendment had specifically caused the drop in judicial bypass cases.
“(Engler) has alleged only that fewer judicial bypass cases have happened to arise in Trumbull County recently,” the ACLU of Ohio wrote in court documents. “That allegation is manifestly insufficient to support an inference that parental consent laws for abortion are no longer being enforced in Ohio.”
The Ohio Supreme Court dismissed the case without filing an opinion explaining the dismissal. The court’s announcement noted that the decision was agreed to by Chief Justice Sharon Kennedy and all six of the other justices on the court.
Abortion rights advocacy group Abortion Forward praised the decision in a recent email newsletter.
“While this case was transparently political, it does provide a valuable example of the potential for judicial interference in abortion politics in Ohio, even with the constitutional guarantee in place,” the newsletter stated.

title: Ohio’s already seen the biggest ACA drop. Premiums are about to go up by another 15%
description: Ohio has seen the biggest enrollment drop of any state since congressional Republicans allowed subsidies for insurance in Affordable Care Act marketplaces to expire, nearly by a third of the half-million Ohioans who bought insurance there dropped it. Now, faced with a smaller, sicker clientele, the 11 insurers remaining in Ohio’s marketplace are proposing to[...]
text:
A man gets a checkup at the Saint Agnes Mobile Health Unit mobile clinic parked at the City Heritage Park in Parlier, Calif., on May 16, 2025. California is one of at least five states plus the District of Columbia that have scaled back state-funded healthcare coverage in response to federal Medicaid cuts and the expiration of Obamacare subsidies. (Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters/CatchLight Local)Ohio has seen the biggest enrollment drop of any state since congressional Republicans allowed subsidies for insurance in Affordable Care Act marketplaces to expire, nearly by a third of the half-million Ohioans who bought insurance there dropped it.
Now, faced with a smaller, sicker clientele, the 11 insurers remaining in Ohio’s marketplace are proposing to increase premiums on average by 14.7% for 2027, according to an analysis by the Center for American Progress. 
Natasha Murphy, the group’s director for health policy, said the new expense will only add to the burden besetting hundreds of thousands of Ohioans who are already struggling to get by.
“It’s just exacerbating the affordability crisis that millions of Americans are finding themselves in — especially as it relates to their monthly premiums,” Murphy told the Capital Journal.
Last summer, congressional Republicans renewed President Donald Trump’s 2017 tax cuts. That was a provision in Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill that provided $1 trillion in cuts for the richest 1% of Americans over 10 years while cutting more than $1 trillion from Medicaid and federal food assistance over the same period.
And while they renewed the tax cuts, congressional Republicans last year declined to renew pandemic-era subsidies for insurance purchased on the ACA exchanges. That caused premiums to more than double for nearly 497,000 Ohioans who bought their health insurance there.
It would have cost about $350 billion to extend the subsidies to 24 million Americans for 10 years. Meanwhile, Trump’s war of choice with Iran has created $38 billion in direct costs in six months — with no end in sight.
After the subsidies expired, 161,000 Ohioans dropped marketplace coverage.
That leaves insurers with customers who are likely to be sicker and more expensive to cover, Murphy said.
“They’re anticipating that the folks who remain in the market are going to be sicker and more expensive,” she said. “A lot of the folks who were healthier — and unfortunately some folks who weren’t that healthy — thought they weren’t able to afford their coverage and dropped out of the marketplace.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.The coverage losses on ACA exchanges come as policymakers are bracing for the brunt of Medicaid cuts to kick in Jan. 1. The Big Beautiful Bill hopes to create the biggest savings by placing bigger paperwork burdens on recipients and restricting states’ ability to raise revenue.
The Congressional Budget Office estimates that the provisions in the Trump bill and the expiration of ACA subsidies will lead to 16 million more Americans being without health insurance by 2034.
Murphy sees the moves as part of a long-term Republican project to undermine the Affordable Care Act, President Barack Obama’s signature legislation — and even Medicaid itself. She called it “death by a thousand cuts.”
“And then when you look at the Medicaid work requirements and what it’s going to take for states to finance their Medicaid programs, it’s a full-throated attack on the ACA,” Murphy said. “But it’s also a pretty significant undermining of Medicaid as a core health-safety net for millions of Americans.” 
If so many Americans lose their insurance, it will have downstream consequences. 
Emergency departments — especially those in rural communities and poor neighborhoods — will be forced to care for more, sicker people who can’t pay. That will force those hospitals to cut services or even close, ER docs warn.
“The unfortunate reality is that hundreds of thousands of Americans have dropped marketplace coverage, many of whom are and will remain uninsured,” Murphy said. “That’s going to have broad implications for individual and family-level health, but more broadly, you’re going to see providers and hospitals see their uncompensated care costs rise and that’s all going to be exacerbated by the upcoming Medicaid changes.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Bipartisan legislative proposals would limit the use of Flock cameras in Pa.
description: Automated license plate readers from Flock Safety and other companies have recently come under fire for potentially abusive surveillance.
text:
An automated license plate reader is seen mounted on a pole on June 13, 2024 in San Francisco, California (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)As public sentiment sours on automatic license plate readers — particularly cameras operated by Flock Safety — state lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are introducing legislation to curtail their use across the commonwealth. 
A trio of bills introduced recently range from an outright ban on fixed cameras to stiffened penalties for unauthorized data access. 
The cameras, known as ALPRs for short, capture images of passing vehicles and upload them to a database police can search. Officers may then use the data to locate vehicles that may be linked to crimes, missing people or other police matters. 
But as the number of law enforcement officers accused of abusing the system has grown, so too have concerns about mass surveillance and privacy violations. 
“There are legitimate circumstances in which this technology can assist law enforcement,” wrote Sen. Doug Mastriano (R-Franklin) in a legislative memo, naming a few examples. “But that is fundamentally different from continuously photographing and recording the movements of every motorist who happens to drive past a camera. Police should investigate people when there is a legitimate reason to suspect wrongdoing. Government should not surveil everyone in hopes of finding wrongdoing.”
His bill would limit permitted uses to stolen vehicles; missing or endangered person alerts; manhunts for “wanted or dangerous” individuals; vehicles “reasonably believed to be connected to a specific criminal investigations”; public safety threats that are “specific and articulable”; warrant searches; and other emergencies with imminent threats to life or safety.
A police officer uses the Flock Safety license plate reader system. Many left-leaning states and cities are trying to protect their residents’ personal information amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, but a growing number of conservative lawmakers also want to curb the use of surveillance technologies. (Photo courtesy of Flock Safety)
Specific language, including proposed penalties and retention rules, hasn’t yet been drafted.
“A police officer with a legitimate reason to look for a particular vehicle should have the tools necessary to do the job. What government should not have is the ability to record the movements of millions of innocent Pennsylvanians simply because someday someone might want to search those records,” Mastriano continued.
A dataset and map compiled by the Electronic Frontier Foundation reports that more than 450 law enforcement agencies in Pennsylvania utilize ALPRs, but doesn’t detail where or how many cameras each organization uses. Some websites have attempted to crowdsource that data, documenting upwards of 2,600 ALPRs across the state. 
 Safety considerations

Earlier this summer, the Washington Post reported that at least 50 law enforcement officers nationwide have been charged or accused of misusing Flock and similar systems to spy on their spouses or intimate partners, exes and their exes’ new partners.
The Post story included an account of a mother from Armstrong County, who said she repeatedly warned police and the district attorney’s office that her police officer husband had used a competitor to Flock to stalk and threaten her. The officer, Michael McSherry, ultimately pleaded guilty to official oppression and served about 11 months in jail, according to the article.
Shortly after, Flock tightened its privacy and oversight controls, recommending data retention for seven days — rather than 30 — and adding tools to restrict data sharing and identify potentially abusive searches. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Referencing the above story, a proposal from Sen. Lisa Boscola (D-Northampton) would “ban knowingly accessing or using an automated surveillance system, or information obtained through such a system, for an unauthorized personal or otherwise unlawful purpose.” 
Individual users would be penalized, though specific language wasn’t immediately available. 
In a recent public post, the Chambersburg Police Department in Franklin County shared its internal guidance for ALPRs from Motorola Solutions, a Flock competitor. Its three fixed cameras and six mobile cameras have been “transformative for community safety,” saying the system has been used in more than 500 criminal investigations since its installation in 2016. 
“An ALPR hit alone is not probable cause for arrest or enforcement action. Officers must independently verify the authenticity of an ALPR hit through law enforcement databases before taking action,” the release continued. 
Additionally, “system inquiries are tracked and limited to legitimate law enforcement purposes,” including associated report numbers and “clear” descriptions of reasoning. “Any misuse would result in departmental discipline and possible criminal violations,” the agency added. 

Flock Safety tightens safeguards as states, cities question surveillance network


The New Castle Police Department in Lawrence County shared its external search logs with the Capital-Star from over a three-year span, comprising more than 11 million records of searches from departments across the country. Its own agency ran just over 10,000 searches in that same period. 
A majority of those searches, more than four out of five, did not list a case number, according to an analysis using an artificial intelligence agent. Many that did had vague or non-descriptive reasons, such as “sus,” “atl,” or “cj.”
Sen. Dan Laughlin (R-Erie) would prohibit “networked” ALPR systems that create automatically databases of every passing vehicle, saying they “could reveal where someone works, worships, receives medical care, spends personal time and who they associate with.” 
The lawmaker was careful to clarify that vehicle-mounted license plate readers would still be allowable. 
“Public safety is a responsibility we all take seriously, but it should not require building a surveillance network capable of tracking the daily movements of millions of innocent individuals,” Laughlin said. “There is a clear difference between an officer using a license plate reader during police work and a permanent network collecting information about everyone who passes by.”
The latest bills are a departure from earlier legislation — one of which would have eased the ability to install cameras on state-owned infrastructure — but align with a House proposal that has seven cosponsors, including one Republican. 
That measure, sponsored by Rep. Tarik Khan (D-Philadelphia), would grant private individuals the right to sue and authorize the state Attorney General’s Office and county district attorneys to investigate violations and bring civil enforcement actions.
At least 16 other states have limited their use, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Data must be deleted in California after 60 days unless it is evidence in a felony case while Vermont requires officers to be certified to access ALPR systems. 
Senior Reporter Peter Hall contributed to this report.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: New law clinic in Georgia aims to keep owners of heirs’ property in their homes
description: A new law clinic at Georgia State University will offer free legal services to help families counter heirs’ property issues, which experts say are a leading cause of involuntary property loss and a barrier to the creation of generational wealth. The problem arises when the owner of a property does not appear on the title, […]
text:
Sarah Stein, an assistant professor at Georgia State University College of Law and the director of the new clinic, spoke at a ribbon cutting ceremony for the clinic in Atlanta on Aug. 27, 2026. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderA new law clinic at Georgia State University will offer free legal services to help families counter heirs’ property issues, which experts say are a leading cause of involuntary property loss and a barrier to the creation of generational wealth.
The problem arises when the owner of a property does not appear on the title, which most commonly happens when someone inherits property from a relative who has passed away without leaving a will. Such property is often split between many different family members, but without clear documentation tying them to a property, families often have a difficult time holding onto their land or accessing services like disaster relief funds that require them to prove ownership of their house.
The problem is particularly acute among low-income households. According to a survey commissioned by the Federal Home Loan Bank of Atlanta, which is pledging $1.5 million to fund the new clinic, about 60% of homeowners nationwide whose household income falls below $50,000 do not have a will, trust or estate plan.
A banner celebrates the opening of a new Georgia State University College of Law clinic seeking to help families counter heirs’ property issues. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
Sarah Stein, an assistant professor at Georgia State University College of Law and the director of the new clinic, said heirs’ property is a “leading cause of Black land loss in the Black Belt” across the South.
The issue can also be seen in urban areas like Atlanta, she added, where developers often disproportionately target families with heirs’ property and urge them to sell their land for below the asking price.
“That pressure on neighborhoods can lead to families deciding to participate in the sale of a home for less money than they would, or in a situation when they wouldn’t otherwise want to lose their home, but they don’t know another option,” Stein said. Rising tax bills or maintenance issues on properties that have fallen into disrepair can lead families to believe that selling their land is the best option, even when other avenues are available.
Part of the clinic’s work, she added, will be in helping families explore all their options, including ones that will allow them to hang onto family property.
“If they don’t have help that is designed to make them aware of all of their options and help them through that process, then they are more likely to fall prey to somebody who has ulterior motives or intentions,” Stein said.
The Heirs’ Property Law Clinic, which plans to begin accepting clients in 2027, aims to both head off the problem by proactively assisting with estate planning and help families resolve existing title issues. Law students at Georgia State University College of Law will provide pro bono legal services to qualifying families.
Congresswoman Nikema Williams, an Atlanta Democrat, spoke at a ribbon cutting ceremony in Atlanta on Aug. 27, 2026. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
Congresswoman Nikema Williams, an Atlanta Democrat, spoke about her own family’s experience navigating heirs’ property issues in neighboring Alabama at a ribbon cutting ceremony for the clinic Thursday evening.
“We figured out how to hold on to that land, but for too many families, that’s just not the case,” she said. “Properties that have been in your family for generations can become difficult to protect when the system doesn’t recognize the way that we have passed down land for generations. You can’t access disaster relief. You can’t make the necessary repairs to your home, and in some cases, you can actually lose it altogether.”
She added that a bill she sponsored, which would allow the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development to help property owners clear their titles and make it easier for those with heirs’ property to access federal disaster aid, recently passed out of committee with bipartisan support. But until there are greater resources to deal with such issues on the federal level, she said, resources like the clinic “will not only be a resource for families seeking support with their properties, but it will also train the next generation of attorneys.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Nixon’s ‘people-powered’ platform propels her to upset win
description: “Pessimists calculate the odds. Optimists believe they can overcome them.” — Ted Koppel State Rep. Angie Nixon’s striking political victory against retired Lt. Col. Alex Vindman in the Aug. 18 Florida Democratic Senate primary election startled pundits and rattled the political establishment in an electoral season marked by a groundswell of voter dissatisfac[...]
text:
Jacksonville Democratic Rep. Angie Nixon speaking in St. Petersburg on Dec. 14, 2025. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)“Pessimists calculate the odds. Optimists believe they can overcome them.” — Ted Koppel
State Rep. Angie Nixon’s striking political victory against retired Lt. Col. Alex Vindman in the Aug. 18 Florida Democratic Senate primary election startled pundits and rattled the political establishment in an electoral season marked by a groundswell of voter dissatisfaction with the status quo and desire for change.
Nixon, an ardent progressive, raised around $975,000 and was outspent 16-1 by Vindman, who raised $16.3 million. Despite the clear financial disadvantage, Nixon’s message, platform, and organizing electrified voters and led to a 12-point shellacking of Vindman, establishment Democrats’ darling.
“We showed the world what organized people can accomplish,” Nixon told supporters on primary night. “And we showed the world what people of Florida are all about. Medicare for all. Universal childcare. Real, affordable housing. Fully funded public education. And an end to senseless wars.”
Nixon, a community organizer and small business owner, refuses to be labeled by the socialist/communist label Republicans have started throwing around.
“Ashley Moody and the corporate politicians of Washington, they like to label us. It’s easier trying to make those afraid of me than to defend the choices they keep making to make our lives harder. They look at this movement and they call us extreme, they call us radical, but I think people see through that. I won’t let them define me and I know you will always know where I stand,” Nixon said.
Nixon’s platform includes universal childcare and pre-K; Medicare for all; free paid family and sick leave; a national rent freeze; a moratorium on evictions; and a universal jobs program with inflation-adjusted wages. She would pay for her policies with taxes on the uber-rich.
“People are working harder than ever and they’re just struggling just to stay afloat,” Nixon said.
 ‘Intense disatisfaction’
The Pew Research Center notes that “voter anger across the United States in 2025 and 2026 has surged, driven by intense dissatisfaction with the national economy, cost-of-living pressures, and profound polarization over federal governance and democratic institutions.”
POLICO’s Kimberly Leonard described Nixon’s triumph this way: “The win in a red state that plays an outsized role in national GOP politics marks one of the progressive movement’s biggest breakthroughs yet this primary season, in part because other successes have been in blue and purple states. But it’s also viewed as a messaging boost in the general election for Republicans, who’ve been eager to tie Democrats across the ballot in Florida to far-left positions.”
Still, lawyer, author, and human rights activist Qasim Rashid was exuberant.
“Angie Nixon just pulled off one of the biggest upsets of 2026. Outspent 20-1. Blocked by the DSCC. Ignored by corporate media. She won anyway — by double digits,” he wrote on Instagram and his Substack account. “Because she listened to what Democratic voters of FL actually believe in, while her opponent refused to even debate her.”
Rashid continued: “When asked why, he said he was focused on November. He won’t be there in November.”
Rashid believes Nixon struck a chord with the electorate.
“She won because the Democratic voters of Florida have been paying attention — to what their party actually believes, to what they have actually been demanding, and to which candidate has actually been listening. This is not a mystery. This is democracy functioning as designed — voters choosing the candidate who represents their actual values, not the candidate the establishment decided was ‘electable’ because he had a famous name and well-funded consultancy operation.”
 Ideological battle
The DSCC decided — without asking Florida Democrats — who the nominee should be, he argues.
“Floridians answered anyway. And the answer was Angie Nixon – by double digits,” he added.
Following her upset, Nixon in an MS NOW interview said she’d raised almost $1 million in the 24 hours since her win. She has been all over the airways spreading her message and her platform, riding the momentum, talking to more voters and knocking on more doors.
Democrats are locked not just in an ideological and generational battle but also a search for their identity that many in the party fear will divide them and give Republicans the opening they need to keep their tenuous hold on Congress. Progressives, democratic socialists, and the voters they are attracting are telling establishment Democrats to lead, follow, or get out the way.
According to Time Magazine’s Nik Popli, socialists have captured or are poised to win mayoralties in Seattle and Washington, DC., while Nithya Raman is headed for a November runoff for mayor in Los Angeles. The DSA could enter the next Congress with its largest contingent ever. Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary with the backing of prominent socialists and a platform that mostly mirrors the DSA’s, although he told Time he doesn’t claim that movement’s mantle.
“For a movement that counted only a few thousand members a decade ago, the transformation is remarkable,” Popli wrote. “Bernie Sanders made democratic socialism legible to millions of Americans; AOC gave it a younger national face; Mamdani demonstrated that a socialist could defeat the Democratic establishment, govern a major city, and then help elect more socialists behind him. But with the midterms looming, the question is now how far the model travels.”
 Progressive victories
Primary elections since 2025 have seen the emergence of progressive and Democratic Socialist candidates: Zohran Mamdani is now running New York City and knocking it out of the park. Chris Rabb. Abdul El Sayid. Darializa Avila Chevalier. Angela Gonzales-Torres. Mai Vang. California State Sen. Aisha Wahab. Their victories have mainstream Democrats apprehensive and troubled.
Remarkably, Democratic leadership is fighting harder against progressives and socialists than against cruel, corrupt Republicans, the Nation’s Anthony Conwright explains.
“If you hate the Democratic Party, then please don’t run for our nomination,” said Jaime Harrison, former chair of the Democratic National Committee, after a slate of DSA-endorsed candidates defeated party incumbents to win Democratic primaries in New York. “Don’t use our resources. Don’t rely on our volunteers. Don’t use our infrastructure. Focus on building the party you actually support.”
Podcaster and political analyst Danielle Moody captured the unease of Democratic voters and those concerned about the dismantling of this country’s institutions and safety net.
People think Democrats “will serve as a firewall against tyranny. We are told that handing the gavel to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries will restore institutional oversight and accountability,” Moody said of what she calls the “faux opposition party.”
“From the poisoned state of our food supply and the resurgence of preventable diseases to the staggering, unaddressed human rights abuses within ICE detention facilities, the public is left wondering where the Democratic leadership actually stands,” Moody wrote.
“Where is the common ground after years of incremental compromise? Nothing about the current political playbook is new; the trajectory was telegraphed years ago. Yet the establishment continues to ask the electorate to trust a strategy of appeasement.”
 Economic concerns
A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll suggests three of four Americans believe the cost of living is headed in the wrong direction; 56% say they’re paying more for gasoline than months ago; meanwhile, 43% of Americans are paying more at the grocery store. The research finds “persistent public anxiety is heavily tied to elevated fuel, energy, and grocery prices driven by ongoing global energy market pressures.”
And a Washington Post/Ipsos poll captures widespread economic concerns that are expected to play an outsize role in the 2026 midterm elections, with Americans remaining pessimistic about the trajectory of the economy and prospects for people like them.
Voters are also troubled as Trump, his family, and co-conspirators loot the American treasury and sell the country for parts; Democrats seem helpless, clutching their pearls and writing sternly worded letters. They want Democrats to fight for them and save their country from the ravenous wolves, and the loyal opposition has failed them.
Voters are striking back with one of the sharpest tools in their arsenal — the vote.
Political pundits who categorically fumbled the ball on Nixon-Vindman tell us Nixon doesn’t stand a chance in November. Nixon, meanwhile, hasn’t eased her foot off the throttle since her win and promises she’ll keep grinding until November.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Congress can finally make progress on this chronic disease
description: Chronic fatigue syndrome affects 38,000 people in Connecticut. Now there's a roadmap to help them.
text:
Patients with one particular disease have heard it over and over: “Your tests came back normal.”
They heard it after the viral infection they never recovered from. They heard it when walking to the mailbox left them bedbound for days. They heard it as their careers ended, their savings drained, and their doctors suggested the problem might be stress. Or anxiety. Or all in their heads.
The disease is myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, or ME/CFS: a serious neuroimmune, neuroinflammatory illness afflicting an estimated 38,000 Connecticut adults. There is no FDA-approved treatment and no validated diagnostic test.
Congress can change that this year. For the first time, a rigorous federal research plan exists: the National Institutes of Health (NIH) ME/CFS Research Roadmap, approved in 2024 and built by scientists, clinicians, and patients. Executing it starts with $50 million in the FY27 appropriations bill. Connecticut’s congressional delegation, with its senior seats on the committees that write that bill, is positioned to deliver it.
The hallmark of ME/CFS is brutal. Even minor exertion, physical or mental, can trigger a crash lasting days, weeks, or months. One in four patients is housebound or bedbound at some point; clinicians compare the disability to end-stage renal disease.
This neglect was never random. ME/CFS affects women three times more often than men, and its history shows what happens when medicine doesn’t believe women.

Dr. Subramani Seetharama

For decades, it was written off as psychosomatic, and the federal research budget followed the stigma. Today, it receives roughly 11 percent of the funding allocated to diseases with a comparable burden — about $13 million a year — even though it affects more people than Parkinson’s and MS combined.
The dismissal follows patients out of the exam room. Women with ME/CFS keep, on average, just 49 percent of their pre-illness income; men keep 63 percent. Women are nearly four times more likely to be denied disability benefits, and frequently report that evaluators simply did not take them seriously.
Patients of every gender spend an average of $4,439 a year out of pocket chasing answers that don’t yet exist. One in five leaves the workforce for good. More than 60 percent depend on unpaid care from parents, spouses, and children — a hidden workload that, once again, falls mostly on women.
If this disease once felt obscure, it no longer is. As many as 45 percent of Long COVID patients meet the diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS, meaning thousands of Connecticut residents who got sick in the last six years and never recovered are living this story too.
That is the problem. The Roadmap is the answer. It lays out concrete priorities: biomarker discovery, a validated diagnostic test, and clinical trials of the most promising treatments. Congress has recognized it and directed NIH to prepare an implementation plan. Only the funding is missing.
This cause belongs to no single party; ME/CFS strikes Democrats and Republicans alike. But I will say plainly, as a Democrat, why this speaks to everything we stand for. We say healthcare is a right — these patients have been locked out of it. We say we believe women — these women were disbelieved for generations, in exam rooms and disability hearings and budget negotiations. We say government should follow the science and deliver for people the system has failed. Here is a chance to prove all of it with a single appropriation.
So I am asking our delegation to use its influence over this bill now. Put $50 million for the ME/CFS Research Roadmap in the FY27 budget.
Somewhere in Connecticut today — in Bridgeport, in Willimantic, in a quiet bedroom with the curtains drawn — someone is hearing those words again: your tests came back normal. What they deserve to hear instead is that their government finally went looking for the test that will come back with the truth.
Dr. Subramani Seetharama is Chief of Rehabilitation Medicine at Hartford Hospital and an assistant professor at UConn School of Medicine.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Generational health is generational wealth
description: To close Connecticut's racial wealth gap, we must start treating health equity as an economic development strategy.
text:
For generations, Black and Brown families were denied equal access to many of the systems that create wealth in America.
Homeownership. Capital. Quality education. Business ownership. Healthcare.
The consequences of those exclusions did not end when the policies changed. They continue to shape who builds wealth, who preserves it, and who is able to pass opportunity to the next generation.
Today, conversations about the racial wealth gap often focus on income, jobs, or entrepreneurship. Those factors matter. But one of the most overlooked drivers of economic mobility is health.
Connecticut cannot meaningfully close racial wealth gaps while ignoring the health disparities that continue to affect Black and Brown communities across our state.
That may sound like a healthcare issue. It is also an economic development issue.

Philip Rigueur

When a family is burdened by chronic illness, preventable disease, untreated mental health challenges, or rising medical costs, resources that could be used for homeownership, education, savings, or entrepreneurship are redirected toward survival. A single health crisis can erase years of financial progress. For communities that have historically faced barriers to wealth-building, those setbacks compound across generations.
Too often, we treat healthcare, education, and economic development as separate challenges. We fund them separately, measure them separately, and debate them separately. Then we wonder why progress on economic mobility remains uneven.The reality is that these issues are deeply interconnected.
Before joining ConnCORP, I spent years working in the healthcare sector. What I learned during that time fundamentally changed how I think about economic development and economic justice.
I saw firsthand that a person’s health often predicts their economic future just as much as their resume. Families burdened by chronic illness, medical debt, untreated mental health conditions, or limited access to care face challenges that extend far beyond the doctor’s office.
Health influences whether a student can succeed in school. It affects whether a parent can maintain steady employment. It shapes whether a family can save money, purchase a home, start a business, or invest for the future.
The consequences compound.
Across Connecticut, many of the communities facing the greatest economic challenges also experience poorer health outcomes, lower homeownership rates, lower educational attainment, and shorter life expectancies. These patterns are not random. They are the result of decades of unequal access to opportunity.
In fact, if you tell me a community’s homeownership rate, I can often make a reasonable prediction about educational outcomes, civic participation, and even life expectancy. The indicators move together because they are connected by the same underlying reality: access. Yet we continue treating them as separate problems requiring separate solutions.
That approach is limiting our ability to make meaningful progress.
If we are serious about creating economic mobility in historically underserved Black and Brown communities, we must start recognizing health as an economic development strategy. For generations, many families were told that hard work alone would create economic opportunity. Hard work remains important. But in today’s economy, wealth is increasingly built through ownership, investment, and assets that compound over time. Health determines whether families are positioned to participate in those systems.
A family struggling with preventable health challenges is often forced to focus on immediate needs rather than long-term wealth creation. Resources that might otherwise support entrepreneurship, education, homeownership, or investment are redirected elsewhere. Healthy families are better positioned to remain employed, pursue education, build businesses, accumulate assets, and pass stability to future generations.
That is why I believe generational health is generational wealth.
When people hear the term “generational wealth,” they often think about money. But families pass down much more than financial assets. They pass down habits, behaviors, knowledge, and expectations. They pass down approaches to nutrition, preventative care, financial decision-making, and long-term planning.
These inheritances may not appear on a balance sheet, but they create value nonetheless. At ConnCORP, our mission is rooted in advancing economic justice and expanding pathways to wealth creation for Black and Brown communities. That work has taught us that wealth is not built through a single intervention. It is built through ecosystems of opportunity. Families need access to quality housing. They need access to education. They need access to healthcare. They need access to ownership and capital. These are not competing priorities. They are mutually reinforcing investments.
When those systems work together, opportunity compounds.
When they don’t, disparities compound instead.
Connecticut has no shortage of conversations about economic development. What we need is a broader understanding of what economic development actually requires.
We cannot close the racial wealth gap while ignoring the health conditions that make wealth-building possible in the first place.
The question is not whether health affects wealth.
The question is whether we are finally willing to treat health equity as an essential part of economic justice.
Because healthier communities are not simply healthier. They are more resilient, more prosperous, and better positioned to create opportunity that lasts for generations.
Philip Rigueur is president of ConnCORP, the Connecticut Community Outreach Revitalization Program.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: As network news turn itself into a ‘Tic Toc platform’ will local television news rise to the challenge?
description: “How is an octopus attaching itself to a swimmer’s face a story on the network news?”
text:
Enjoying a lazy afternoon lunch on the Connecticut shore, a friend turns to me and says, “network news has become a Tic Toc platform.” 
With a smirk he adds, “How is an octopus attaching itself to a swimmer’s face a story on the network news?” Knowing I spent my career as a television news reporter, he adds, “I get much more information from local news.” 


My buddy is a neurologist in the Philadelphia area with wide interests including local issues, politics and especially sports. He’s not wrong about network news.
Snap on the evening newscast for ABC, NBC, or CBS and your likely to get a smattering of competent reporting from the White House, Justice Department or Supreme Court followed by cascades of video of flooding, damaging winds, and heavy rain from across the county without a mention of why the atmosphere is so vicious spawning heavy storms or bone dry conditions. 
The words climate change are seemly banned from the newscasts especially out of the mouths of meteorologists standing along the Hudson River, just outside New York City , to preview the wild weather sure to come.
The remainder of the newscasts is easily predictable. A picture of a young girl bitten by a barracuda requiring stiches while on vacation. A shark bite of a man swimming in tropical waters causing minor injuries. A fiery crash of a small plane into a home in which no one is injured. All these images are dramatic if not important. And, yes, the frightened octopus with bad aim attaching itself to a fisherman before being pulled off and tossed away.
 All of this presents a gaping hole for local television news to rumble through if station owners, now free to corral as many local stations as they can scoop up, are bold enough to do it.
Local television newsrooms can be staffed with reporters, editors and photographers who know the community and are committed to tell their stories. They have contacts and know the context of how past events impact daily stories. In Connecticut, during the recent primary election, the local TV stations competently covered the dramatic win by Luke Bronin in the First Congressional District over 28-year incumbent John Larson. WTNH, ABC in New Haven, offered not one but two debates for both the congressional race and the Democratic primary for governor won by Ned Lamont over challenger Josh Elliot. Proving strong local journalism can be done but it takes effort and a commitment of money.
Unfortunately, the trends don’t look good. Industry observers report a drop in local tv employment in 2025 a trend continuing in 2026 as fewer ownership groups merge to control more tv outlets and others impose wholesale layoffs in a push to streaming and centralized production of news for multiple communities. Some newsrooms are replacing full time, experienced journalists with part-time, less experienced staff earning far lower wages with no benefits.
There is a way out.
The popularity of podcasts clearly shows audiences want smart, deep-dive content. Local TV news can provide that with robust, experienced staff and a full commitment by management to smart, aggressive, fearless coverage.
 It can work.
If you want to see where it doesn’t, turn to network news in its present form and the octopus. It’s not a fearful creature from the deep, just a scared mollusk hanging on for dear life.
Jeffrey Cole of Madison is a former news anchor for WFSB in Hartford and more recently retired as an investigative reporter at Fox 29 in Philadelphia.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Amazon changes course on water use for Virginia data center campus
description: Amazon Web Services is changing course on how a planned King George County data center will get its water, after a proposal to renew a groundwater permit for withdrawals of up to 6.4 million gallons annually from the Potomac aquifer raised concerns.
text:
The Gov. Harry W. Nice Memorial/Sen. Thomas “Mac” Middleton Bridge carries U.S. Route 301 over the Potomac River, connecting Charles County, Maryland, with King George County, Virginia. The old bridge, in the background, was demolished shortly after the new bridge opened in 2022. (Photo courtesy the Maryland Transportation Authority)Amazon Web Services is changing course on how a King George County data center project will get its water after an application to renew a groundwater permit allowing withdrawals of up to 6.4 million gallons annually from the Potomac aquifer raised concerns.
The tech giant is set to construct a major data center campus in the county at the Birchwood Drive tech campus that could host more than a dozen data centers across the 869-acre property. The county is located across the Potomac from Charles County, Md.
While some of the project is currently tied up in court proceedings, an application to renew a water permit for the tech campus led Sen. Richard Stuart (R-King George) to urge the Department of Environmental Quality to deny the application.
The permit would have allowed the facility to withdraw water from the aquifer that would not be used for cooling the data centers, but rather for employee use, grounds management and other purposes.
But the application came on the heels of a DEQ report that laid out a stark warning that groundwater east of Interstate 95 is “declining [in] availability in the near future,” and that the aquifer would not be able to handle any major new permits for water withdrawals.
“They do not need to drill a well into the aquifer, particularly since we finally got my water study released, which shows us … that we’re in a critical stage with regard to the Potomac aquifer,” Stuart told The Mercury.
Amazon abandons plans for data center campus at Calvert Cliffs

The report has led to policy discussions over how the commonwealth can preserve the Potomac aquifer, a critical water source for the eastern portion of the state.
Following the release of the eastern groundwater availability report, a group of lawmakers has called on Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger to convene a special session to pass legislation aimed at protecting the resource ahead of the General Assembly’s regular session in January. Spanberger has not publicly responded to this request.
Stuart wrote a scathing letter to DEQ noting that the department has directed the county to reduce its reliance on the aquifer and switch to surface water from the Rappahannock River as its primary source of drinking water. Stuart said allowing a massive company like Amazon to use the water instead of preserving it for human consumption should not be allowed.
“The (Virginia) Constitution guarantees the natural resources for the benefit and enjoyment of the citizens. We do not have any extra water,” Stuart said. “Why in the world would they allow Amazon to withdraw water from the aquifer and force a county of 29,000 people, a small rural county, to spend $70 to $100 million to get water from the river and require treatment?”
While 6.4 million gallons over the course of one year may seem like a lot, the permit would not have come close to cracking the top five industrial water users from the Potomac aquifer. The top two users, according to DEQ records, are two paper mills: Global Cellulose Fibers in Franklin, which is permitted to withdraw 6.4 billion gallons annually, and WestRock CP LLC, which may use up to 6.3 billion gallons.
Stuart said that it did not matter that the Amazon permit would be dwarfed by other permits. He said the report shows that new withdrawals should not be considered in order to preserve drinking water for Virginians.
Amazon responded by saying it is looking at alternatives.
“We take concerns of the community seriously and plan to seek alternate water sources as advised by VDEQ and Virginia regulation,” a spokesperson for the tech giant told The Mercury. “We prioritize minimizing water use, and that’s why we invest in infrastructure to utilize reclaimed water across the commonwealth and continuously work to make our data centers more water efficient.”
Amazon is in the process of withdrawing its application for the groundwater withdrawal permit.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana Democrats make endorsements in congressional races
description: The Louisiana Democratic Party has selected the candidates it will officially back in the Nov. 3 congressional midterm elections
text:
Lindsay "Rubia" Garcia speaks with reporters Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026, after qualifying for the 6th Congressional District race at the State Archives in Baton Rouge. (Photo by Elise Plunk/Louisiana Illuminator)The Louisiana Democratic Party has selected the candidates it will officially back in the Nov. 3 congressional midterm elections, when Republicans will be heavily favored to retain five of the state’s six seats they hold in the U.S. House of Representatives.
The Democratic State Executive Committee endorsed Lindsay “Rubia” Garcia of Walker over two other party members — Chauna Banks and Pat Forbes — in the race for the new 6th District. Forbes, the former head of the state Office of Community Development, had received the backing of his former boss, Gov. John Bel Edwards, upon qualifying Aug. 6.
Garcia was the state party’s pick in the former 5th District before Gov. Jeff Landry issued an executive order that removed U.S. House races from the May 15 party primary ballot. She is a plaintiff in a federal lawsuit challenging the order, though her case remains in legal limbo.
“Humbled. Honored. And completely ready to work,” Garcia, a former teacher and Southern University law school graduate, said in a news release Saturday from her campaign.
State Rep. Pat Moore of Monroe received the Louisiana Democratic Party’s endorsement in the 5th District race over Bunkie lawyer Dan McKay and Tallulah contractor Antonio Wilson. Moore has held her legislative seat since 2019. 
John Day, a professional writer and U.S. Navy veteran from Lake Charles, won the endorsement for the 3rd District race over Lafayette lawyer Priscilla Gonzales. 
Conrad Cable, a Union Parish farmer, was the Democrats’ choice in the 4th District race over Shreveport educator Matt Gromlich. 
Louisiana’s congressional elections are being decided through an open “jungle” primary with candidates from all parties placed on the ballot. The state diverted from its new semi-closed party primary system after a landmark U.S. Supreme Court decision in April on a Louisiana redistricting case opened the door for state lawmakers to redraw its U.S. House districts. 
The new versions, along with Landry’s executive order to suspend the U.S. House races in May,   effectively ended the reelection bid of U.S. Rep. Cleo Fields, D-Baton Rouge, in the 6th District. 
The lone remaining Democrat in Louisiana’s congressional delegation, 2nd District U.S. Rep. Troy Carter of New Orleans, does not face any opponents from his own party. Nor does Metairie teacher Lauren Jewett, who is challenging House Majority Leader Steve Scalise in the 1st District 
In what’s been an unconventional endorsement process, the Louisiana Republican Party has backed two candidates in the 6th District: state Sens. Rick Edmonds in Baton Rouge and Blake Miguez of New Iberia.
The Louisiana GOP has backed Board of Regents chair Misti Cordell of Monroe in the 5th District, though it has not closed the door on additional endorsements. Other Republicans in the race include state Reps. Mike Echols of Monroe and Gabe Firment of Pollock, and state Sen. Stewart Cathey of Monroe.
U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson is a heavy favorite to keep his seat in the 4th District as is U.S. Rep Clay Higgins in the 3rd District.

name: VTDigger
title: Schools in Barre start the year without a district budget
description:
Voters in the city of Barre and Barre town have rejected the district’s proposed budgets twice. Now an even tighter budget will be up for a vote next month.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Schools in Barre start the year without a district budget.
text:
The Barre City Elementary and Middle School seen in August 2023. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

As kids across the city of Barre and Barre town returned to class this week, their school district spanning the two municipalities still doesn’t have a voter approved budget. 
Voters in the district shot down two proposed budgets this spring — first in March, then again in May — leaving the Barre Unified Union School District as the only district in the state without a budget.
Now, voters are set to decide on Sept. 15 if they will approve a tighter spending plan for this year. 
At the heart of the budget rejections is the fact that school spending in the district is set to impact each municipality differently this year. In the city of Barre, residents are looking at a 25-27% decrease in property tax rates, while residents of Barre town are looking at property tax increases dependent on the town’s school spending, according to Garrett Grant, the board’s chair. 
About 61% of voters who rejected the district’s budget in May were from Barre town, data shows. 
The district similarly started the school year without a budget in 2024 before voters later approved a spending plan on their fourth attempt. Passing a school budget is a perennial challenge in the district, according to Grant, who said the struggle predates his five years living in the city. 
And after that rejection, the school’s board decided to cut the budget even more. 
The board’s new proposed $57.1 million budget increases district spending by 2.1% compared to last year. It cuts $350,000 in district costs compared to the budget rejected in May. 
As long as the district lacks a voter approved budget, it has to take out a line of credit to keep its doors open, according to Superintendent Emilie Knisley. Districts without an approved spending plan are allowed to spend up to 87% of their previous year’s budget, but the district also has to pay additional interest payments to a local bank, Knisley said. 
Those interest payments could cost up to $22,000 each month, according to Knisley. 
“If we can’t come to some sort of agreement on what spending should be and get a budget passed, it becomes more and more expensive,” she said. 
Grant said he thinks the controversy over school spending is fueled in part by Vermonters’ growing concerns over affordability. And school spending gives people a rare opportunity to have a say over their costs of living, he said. 
“I didn’t get a vote for gas prices to go up. I didn’t get a vote for my utility bills and my groceries to go up. But you do get a vote on the school budget,” Grant said. 
Plus, Gov. Phil Scott, who has fiercely advocated for cutting education costs, is from Barre. “People listen to him in Barre,” Grant said, referring to the governor. 
Grant also attributed the budget failures to misinformation about how the district calculates its spending. 
There’s a false idea that the school board hasn’t gone through its budget line by line, he said, and is accounting for “phantom” students. 
Every time the board has slimmed down its budget this year ahead of a vote, it’s had to make cuts to existing programs or personnel, Grant said. So far, it’s nixed the district’s summer school program, it’s decided not to fill vacant teaching positions and it combined some resources between schools. 
Even before those efforts to cut costs, the district spends less per student than surrounding districts Paine Mountain and Montpelier, according to Knisley. 
The debate in town has been divisive at times, Knisley said, and has left those on both sides of the debate feeling frustrated. 
Grant said he’s optimistic the district might pass its budget next month and is trying to encourage more residents to vote. The district is hosting an informational meeting on Sept. 8 in the library of Spaulding High School. 
If the budget doesn’t pass next month, Grant said the district will have to look at cutting spending on transportation, athletics and extracurricular activities. 
“That’s not what I want. I don’t think that’s what the board wants. I don’t think that’s what our admin wants, but that’s kind of the reality we’re in right now,” he said.

name: VTDigger
title: Sen. Welch meets with Vermont farmers to discuss rural economic crisis
description:
Vermont farmers met with Sen. Peter Welch to discuss land ownership barriers, USDA delays, and the urgent need for stable food policies.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Sen. Welch meets with Vermont farmers to discuss rural economic crisis.
text:
Fresh tomatoes growing at Honey Fields farm in Norwich Vt.Photo by Molly Hughes/Valley News

This story by Molly Hughes was first published in the Valley News on Aug.27, 2026.NORWICH — Vermont farmers can’t afford to own the land they farm, and the federal money meant to help them has become a paperwork contest that pays out late, if at all.
Those were the two problems that came up most when six farmers sat down Thursday at Honey Field Farm in Norwich with U.S. Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., in a two-hour roundtable organized by the Northeast Organic Farming Association of Vermont.
“It’s so funny that we hear about this farm bill and the people arguing it,” said Amy Huyffer, of the Strafford Creamery. “The question they should start with is, ‘Did I eat today, and do I want to eat tomorrow?’”
For Eli and Valerie Hersh, who run Honey Field Farm, the idea of ownership is still aspirational. The couple took over the vegetable and nursery operation seven years ago through a lease-to-own arrangement with Dirt Capital Partners, a private investment firm that bought the farm when the Hershes couldn’t. They hope to complete the purchase next summer. 
“It kind of illustrates the need for so many different methods of doing that farm transfer, so that this farm, which is such a legacy, could continue as a farm,” Eli Hersh said.
That barrier was the through-line of the morning.
“We don’t own any of the land we farm,” said Shona Sanford-Long, who runs Flying Dog Farm in Tunbridge and started her livestock business in 2020 with animals from her parents’ farm and no savings. 
She said her generation is trying to build ownership structures that don’t come with “that huge burden of a mortgage that makes everything else impossible” — while also covering the fencing, water lines and barns it takes just to begin.
Her mother, Suzanne Long, has run Luna Bleu Farm in South Royalton since the 1980s and is now working on the same problem from the other end. She and her husband are renovating a smaller house on the property so they can hand over the one they live in to a poultry-farming couple who have been land-insecure for at least five years.
Their transition is part of a broader effort through the White River Land Collaborative, a Tunbridge-based nonprofit organization, to keep local farmland in production as older farmers age out.
“How can this farm that we work so hard to build, and these soils that we work so hard to build, still continue to be a farm and be an asset to the next generation?” she said.
Long said the trap runs in both directions: Older farmers whose only wealth is their land and barns can’t afford to leave, and younger farmers who came up through the system can’t afford to buy in. 
“You have to have other money, family money — or else have a different kind of job, and then come to farming,” she said. “But for those folks that have come up through farming, it’s really tough.”
The federal programs meant to ease that squeeze are, farmers said, increasingly unreliable.
Sanford-Long described a fencing contract funded through the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service that was supposed to be installed last fall. Since the money comes as reimbursement, the government shutdown stalled it — but she had already paid a deposit and couldn’t front the rest. The project slipped to spring. Payments on newer work have been delayed again, she said, this time by USDA restructuring and staff eliminations.
Even approved grants can sit unused for years, she said, because farms don’t have the cash to spend first and wait to be reimbursed. And the applications themselves have started to crowd out the work.
“That’s what farming is becoming,” she said. “It’s like, ‘OK, how good of a grant writer am I? How well can I fit my story into what the grant is asking for?’”
Welch was blunt about the USDA staffing shortage behind the delays. “Right now, they’re supposed to be staffed at 47 people, and they’ve got — nine,” he said. “That is horrifying.”

READ MORE

He said he planned to stop by the state office that afternoon to thank the people still there.
Underneath the access problems is the issue of pricing. Nationally, farmers received just 11.8 cents of every dollar Americans spent on domestically produced food in 2024, according to USDA’s Economic Research Service. After production expenses, farmers and ranchers kept about 5.8 cents, per an American Farm Bureau Federation analysis of the same data. 
Stephen Leslie, of Cedar Mountain Farm and Cobb Hill Cheese in Hartland, pointed to dairy: milk prices “flatlined” by 1993, he said, while costs to produce it kept climbing — a gap that hasn’t closed since.
Long put it in consumer terms. “Everyone’s talking about how expensive eggs are,” she said. “The conversation is all about ‘We can’t afford to eat,’ but the farmers can’t afford to produce food at that price.”
Sanford-Long said farmers absorb the difference themselves. Any of them could pivot to a high-end specialty product that actually covers costs, she said, “but then if the goal is to actually feed people, the people we want to feed aren’t going to be able to afford that.”
Welch traced the gap to consolidation beyond the farm gate. The Farm Bill mostly subsidizes equipment, seed and fertilizer companies, he said in an interview, and the challenge is “to reorient the Farm Bill towards feeding America nutritious foods and producing it locally, as opposed to just providing subsidies to Big Ag.”
That pressure carries a human cost. Valerie Hersh, who had worked with the federal Farmer and Rancher Stress Assistance Network, told Welch that farmers “historically have one of the highest suicide rates of any occupation,” and said a national mental-health program serving farmers and farmworkers, Cultivemos, was ended by a stop-work order last year. 
A 2023 CDC report found male farmers, ranchers and agricultural managers died by suicide at a rate of 52 per 100,000, compared with 32 per 100,000 among men in other occupations. 
There is no comparable data from women in farming. 
Long said the strain gets internalized. “You keep saying, ‘How come after 10 years I’m still struggling? How come after 15 years? How come after 20 years? What am I doing wrong? I must not be good enough,’” she said. 
Several farmers proposed a structural answer: guaranteed income. 
“Universal Basic Income for farmers who are able and willing to adopt organic, regenerative practices,” Leslie said, framing it as payment for ecological repair as much as for food. 
Eli Hersh said farmworkers get left out of the conversation entirely. Honey Field’s top wage is about $25 an hour, which he said isn’t enough for someone to build a life, and the farm gets by on part-timers who farm elsewhere, too. He said talented young people cycle through and leave for jobs that can cover student loans.
“It’s devastating to think about your kids having interest in farming, but knowing that you can’t, with good conscience, recommend it as a career option when it’s the most vital career that someone should have,” he said.
Labor pressure on Vermont farms isn’t only about wages. The state’s dairy sector relies heavily on immigrant workers — roughly 1,200 to 1,500, according to a study done by the University of Vermont.
Asked afterward about stepped-up immigration enforcement, Welch called it “outrageous” and “destructive,” and said it is “really hurting our farm community.” He said the country can and must have a legitimate farm labor program instead.
The biggest obstacle to passing the bill is a fight over nutrition funding. Republicans’ tax and spending package cut benefits by hundreds of billions of dollars, and Welch said he is pushing to restore the longstanding link between farm programs and nutrition programs.
Huyffer said she doesn’t want the Agriculture Committee to be moved by sympathy. She recalled a Washington event where farmers’ hardship stories were read aloud to staffers, and said that framing gets it backward.
“I don’t want Sen. Welch or anybody in the ag community to take care of us because we’re a sad story, or even an admirable story,” she said. “I would like people to have sustainable food policy because they want to eat tomorrow, and they want to eat next year, and they want their kids to be able to eat in 20 years.”

name: VTDigger
title: White River Valley Supervisory Union addresses chronic absenteeism through community connections
description:
Administrators find that working in the community can be just what chronically absent students need.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  White River Valley Supervisory Union addresses chronic absenteeism through community connections.
text:
Students of WRVMS stand in front of their fence built at Metcalf Cemetery in Royalton. Photo by Caitlin Justice/White River Valley Herald

This story by Caitlin Justice was first published in The White River Valley Herald on Aug. 27, 2026.After battling high absentee rates after the Covid-19 pandemic, schools in the White River Valley Supervisory Union are finding ways to keep kids in schools and build community connections. According to Michaela Martin, the SU’s multi-tiered system of support coordinator, working in the community can be just what chronically absent students need.
In 2024, the WRVSU and a few other supervisory unions in the region received a grant through UVM called Everyday Counts to help bring these high absenteeism rates back down.
Since implementing the Everyday Counts Grant, most schools in the WRVSU district now maintain a daily attendance of 90% or higher. Of the district’s 10 schools, three have not reached this threshold. Two of those are on the cusp of 90% daily attendance, while the high school’s absence rates still hovers around the 20% mark. Prior to the pandemic, WRVSU logged a chronic absenteeism rate of 10.51% over all of its schools. In 2022, chronic absenteeism doubled to 20.56%. This past year the supervisory union has been able to get these rates even lower than the pre-pandemic mark — 6.92% throughout WRVSU.
Since the year-long grant ended, Martin has been helping to continue the work to address chronic absenteeism even without funding from the grant.
“Anytime you do an initiative like this, you have to sustain it,” Martin said.
According to Martin, the first step of tackling this attendance issue was identifying the barrier. 
She said students have many different reasons for being absent from school, such as illness or transportation issues. For many students, however, it’s due to negative peer interactions or lack of connection at school. One way to address that situation is to help those students feel connected to their community.
“You have to find what works for kids and what they are motivated to do,” Martin said.
Heather Leavitt, one of the cemetery commissioners in Royalton, reached out to WRVHS for help building a fence for the cemetery. Martin took on the project and selected students from the middle school who struggle with truancy, hoping that seeing a physical result from their work would motivate them to come to school.
“Once they saw the fence being developed and they could actually see their work, they were more eager to come to school because it was going to help someone else,” Martin said. “So a lot of times students just want to help and see their impact on their community.”
Leavitt came out while they were building the fence and gave them cake to thank them for their help.
“They saw that their work really mattered to someone else,” Martin said.
Through the grant, WRVSU also connected with a local horse farm, giving students the opportunity to learn about the anatomy of horses and how to care for them. Martin said this motivated students to come to school because they loved the experience, and many students are interested in animals.
“So it’s those kinds of things that if we’re struggling with students, in getting them to school, then how do we incentivize, motivate them to come and see it as something that’s worthwhile?” Martin said.

READ MORE

Since these projects, Martin has met with Leavitt to discuss other ways students can help their community. Martin wants to find a way to build an educational program where students are able to work on projects, such as the cemetery fence, while connecting history, geography, and language arts to these projects, which would allow students to receive class credit for their work.
“That’s our belief system,” Martin said, “that community schools are where kids thrive and how do we create opportunities within their own community to not only help support, but also learn through their community instead of sitting in a class.”
To be considered chronically absent, a student must be absent 10% of the school year, Martin said.
According to national research, missing 10% of school days is tied to lower educational and health outcomes, lower graduation rates, and shorter life expectancy.
She said it is important to catch chronic absenteeism early, before it becomes habitual and a harder problem to solve. Once kids become older and enter high school, redirecting them becomes a bigger challenge. Identifying barriers to attendance and setting up a plan for students to be successful has helped address the issue significantly in WRVSU, she said.
“It’s just really about getting to the root cause of why they don’t want to come to school,” Martin said.
This upcoming year, Martin said the goal is to begin focusing on students who are frequently tardy. She said if students habitually come to school an hour late every day, they are missing essential parts of their day. She wants to find ways to support these students in getting out of the house in the morning.
“Our end goal is graduation,” she emphasized. “So how do we work together to make sure that that happens?”

name: VTDigger
title: Short-term rentals are vital to Vermont’s economy
description:
Blaming vacation rentals for the housing crisis overlooks who’s actually paying more.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Short-term rentals are vital to Vermont’s economy.
text:
This commentary is by Jenny Dewar, who has lived in Pownal for 20 years and is a board member of the Vermont Short-Term Rental Alliance.
I am writing in response to recent letters by Donna Brown and Lew Holzman, who have both contributed to the vilification of short-term rentals in defense of their second homes in Vermont. 
There is a lot to unpack in their letters. Both are part-timers. This is a tradition in Vermont for people from New York and elsewhere who enjoy their country weekend or vacation homes. I have no problem with them whatsoever. Their taxes and presence are vital to rural communities.
It’s lucky for Brown that she is in a financial position to own her second home without having to rent it out short-term. She wrote, “We did not cause this housing situation because we have a well-used vacation home. We do not rent it out as a short-term rental. Friends and family come and use it.” Cool.
We did not cause this housing shortage either. I own, and now live in, a large house left to me unexpectedly by my parents, who didn’t leave any money to pay the mortgage. I manage another that is still enjoyed by the family who grew up in it. I do not have Brown’s luck to afford it without inviting short-term guests. 
Neither house would be viable for first-time homeowners unless they had an enormous chunk of change burning a hole in their pockets, and neither could be kept if we could not also use them as short-term rentals. If or when we sell them, they will likely go to other second-home owners or Vermonters who rent them out to afford them. 
Holzman wrote, “We pay our taxes but are on a fixed income, so increases are a concern. What about short-term rentals like Airbnbs, which need to be regulated and taxed at a higher rate? Wouldn’t it be more meaningful to try to attract more businesses to Vermont and make them pay their fair share of taxes?”
Well, firstly, we pay extraordinarily high property taxes, and increases are a major concern for us as well.
Secondly, the phrase “short-term rentals like Airbnbs” uses language that I find irritating. My business is my business, and it is a short-term rental. Airbnb is simply one of the platforms we use to attract guests. I do not own an Airbnb. I simply use the platform, just as I use Vrbo and my own website.
Finally, we are already taxed at a higher rate. Our guests pay an extra 3% surcharge on top of the 9% base Vermont meals and rooms tax, for a total of 12%. We are the only lodging industry in Vermont with this additional tax. Does that drive guests to hotels? Nope. It drives them to the Berkshires, New Hampshire, Maine and upstate New York. 
So how does that equate to the accusation that we do not pay our “fair share” of taxes? 
Holzman also wrote, “How will the taxing authorities identify who comes to Vermont once in a while versus those of us who come regularly and spend our money at the general stores, restaurants and many recreational establishments?”

READ MORE

Short-term rentals in our state are occupied full time. While a specific guest may only come once in a while, I personally host hundreds — if not thousands — of guests every year. Believe me, they are spending money at general stores, downtown restaurants and recreational establishments in Vermont because that is where I send them. Several additional small-business owners benefit: mowers, plow operators, cleaners, handy people, electricians, yoga instructors, massage therapists, home chefs and so on — all folks I recommend to my guests to enrich their stays. 
I am not different or special. I am on the board of the Vermont Short-Term Rental Alliance, and we hold a yearly conference where owners come together to learn, share ideas and study how to make our spaces safe and responsible. We contribute to the economy through property taxes, meals and rooms taxes, and funneling guests to local establishments. 
Our properties probably put more money into the economy than second-home owners when compared directly. That said, collectively we have far fewer properties. The data says we own around 3% to 4% of the housing stock. 
We are not the enemy. We are not the problem. We are not attacking second-home owners. I wish they would return the courtesy.

title: ‘Unbearable’ heat in uncooled Alabama prisons
